posts.title: Contextual Retrieval: Fixing RAG's Context-Free Chunks
posts.subtitle: A short LLM-written blurb per chunk can cut retrieval failures by up to two-thirds
posts.summary: Chunking a document for RAG strips away the surrounding context each chunk needs to be found. Contextual Retrieval fixes this by having an LLM prepend a short, chunk-specific summary before embedding and keyword-indexing — and prompt caching keeps the cost low enough to run over an entire corpus.

slides.title: Your chunks forgot what document they're from
slides.body: Split a 50-page filing into 200-token chunks and most of them read like orphaned sentences. Embeddings can only match what's on the page — and a page that says 'revenue grew 3%' with no company or quarter attached is nearly unsearchable.

slides.title: Chunking trades recall for indexability
slides.body: You chunk because embedding a whole document blurs it into a mushy average vector that matches everything and nothing. But small chunks lose the referents — pronouns, company names, dates, section headers — that a query actually searches on.
bullets: A chunk reading 'the company's revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter' has no company, no year, no filing type
Standard fixes — bigger chunks, sliding windows, overlap — trade the same problem for a blurrier one
The failure is silent: retrieval just returns the wrong top-k, and nothing in the pipeline flags it

slides.title: Prepend context before you index, not after you retrieve
slides.body: For every chunk, an LLM reads the chunk alongside the full source document and writes a 1-2 sentence blurb that situates it — then that blurb is glued onto the chunk before it goes into both the embedding index and the keyword (BM25) index.
bullets: Prompt: 'here is the whole document; here is one chunk from it; write brief context to situate this chunk for search retrieval'
The generated context is prepended, not appended — it becomes part of what gets embedded
It also gets indexed into BM25, so exact keyword matches (part numbers, tickers, names) improve too, not just semantic ones

slides.title: Prompt caching is what makes this affordable
slides.body: Naively, re-contextualizing every chunk means re-sending the whole document once per chunk — a document with 100 chunks gets read 100 times. Caching the document as a shared prefix and only varying the chunk in each call turns that into one long-context read plus 100 cheap cache hits.
bullets: Without caching: cost scales with (chunks × document length) — expensive for long documents
With prompt caching: the document is written to cache once, each chunk-context call reuses it near-free
Anthropic reported roughly $1.02 per million document tokens processed this way — cheap enough to run over a full corpus, not just a sample

slides.title: Each layer you add compounds the gain
slides.body: Anthropic's own eval (top-20 chunk retrieval failure rate, averaged across several codebases and knowledge bases) showed the gains stack rather than substitute for each other.

slides.title: Same sentence, before and after
slides.body: The chunk's raw text never changes — you're not summarizing it away, you're wrapping it.
bullets: Raw chunk: 'The company's revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter.'
Generated context: 'This chunk is from an SEC filing on ACME Corp's Q2 2023 performance; the previous quarter refers to Q1 2023.'
Indexed text: context + raw chunk — now a query for 'ACME Q2 2023 revenue growth' has real terms to match on, in both the vector index and BM25

slides.title: Where it doesn't pay off
slides.body: This is an indexing-time cost for a retrieval-time gain — it's the wrong trade in a few cases.
bullets: Small corpora that already fit in a single context window: skip retrieval entirely, just stuff the whole thing in the prompt
Highly dynamic corpora: every edit means re-contextualizing and re-indexing affected chunks, so update-heavy stores pay this cost repeatedly
Cheap or low-quality context-generation prompts produce generic blurbs ('this chunk discusses financial results') that add tokens without adding signal — the context has to actually be specific
It improves recall, not reasoning — a retrieval system that finds the right chunk but hands it to a weak generator still produces a weak answer

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Chunking for RAG throws away the context a chunk needs to be found — contextual retrieval writes that context back in before indexing
It touches both indexes: contextual embeddings for semantic match, contextual BM25 for exact keyword match
Prompt caching is the enabler — without it, re-reading the full document per chunk makes this too expensive to run at corpus scale
Stack it with reranking for the largest combined gain; each layer addresses a different failure mode
Best fit for large, relatively stable corpora where retrieval quality — not update latency — is the bottleneck

questions.prompt: What does contextual retrieval actually change about a chunk before it's indexed?
options: It shortens the chunk to remove redundant words
It prepends a short LLM-generated blurb that situates the chunk within its source document
It translates the chunk into a canonical schema
It replaces the chunk's text with its embedding vector
questions.explanation: The raw chunk text is preserved; a short situating blurb (e.g. which document, company, time period) is generated and prepended, then both pieces are indexed together — into the embedding index and the BM25 keyword index.

questions.prompt: Why is prompt caching essential to making this technique practical?
options: It makes the embedding model faster at query time
It avoids re-sending the full source document on every single chunk's context-generation call
It compresses the vector index to save storage
It lets you skip generating context for short chunks
questions.explanation: Without caching, generating context for every chunk means resending the whole document each time — cost scales with chunks × document length. Caching the document once as a shared prefix turns that into one full read plus cheap cache hits per chunk.

questions.prompt: Based on the reported failure-rate numbers, which combination produced the largest reduction over baseline embeddings?
options: Contextual embeddings alone (-35%)
Contextual embeddings + contextual BM25 (-49%)
Contextual embeddings + BM25 + reranking (-67%)
BM25 alone, no embeddings
questions.explanation: The gains compound: contextual embeddings cut the failure rate by 35%, adding contextual BM25 brought it to 49%, and stacking a reranking step on top brought the combined reduction to 67% versus the embeddings-only baseline.

posts.title: Prompt Caching: Paying Full Price to Re-Read the Same Prefix
posts.subtitle: Why re-sending an identical 40K-token system prompt on every turn is the most avoidable cost in an LLM app
posts.summary: Prompt caching reuses a model's stored key/value activations for a prefix that hasn't changed, so a repeated system prompt or tool schema gets skipped instead of reprocessed. It turns cost and latency from scaling with total prompt length into scaling with just the new tokens — but only if the prefix matches byte-for-byte and you reuse it inside the cache's TTL.

slides.title: You're Paying to Re-Read the Same Prompt Every Turn
slides.body: A coding agent that ships a 40,000-token system prompt with every request pays for those 40,000 tokens again on turn two, turn three, and every turn after — even though nothing in them changed.

slides.title: Every Call Reprocesses the Full Prompt From Token Zero
slides.body: A transformer computes attention over every token in the input, every single call. Without caching, the model has no memory that it already saw this exact prefix a second ago.
bullets: A support bot with a 30K-token policy doc + tool schema pays for those 30K tokens on every one of 10,000 daily requests
Cost and latency scale with total prompt length, not with the handful of new tokens the user actually added
Multi-turn agents resend the entire growing transcript each turn — the waste compounds as the conversation gets longer

slides.title: Cache the KV Activations for a Prefix, Not the Text
slides.body: The first call computes and stores the key/value activations for a prefix. Any later call whose prompt starts with that identical prefix skips recomputing attention for those tokens and processes only what's new.
bullets: Providers let you mark 'cache breakpoints' — points in the prompt (end of system instructions, end of tool defs) up to which the prefix should be cached
The match is exact and positional: caching operates on the literal token sequence from position zero, not on meaning or similarity
A cache hit means the model only runs the expensive forward pass on the suffix — the new user turn

slides.title: Cache Reads Are Cheap; Cache Writes Cost a Bit More
slides.body: Every major provider prices a cache write above the base input rate and a cache read well below it — the discount is the entire incentive to restructure your prompt around a stable prefix.

rows: explicit caches: minutes to hours, set by you

slides.title: Worked Example: A Support Agent's Per-Turn Bill
slides.body: Say the shared prefix (system prompt + tool schemas + policy doc) is 40,000 tokens and each user turn adds 200 new tokens.
bullets: Uncached: every turn reprocesses all 40,200 tokens — cost and latency stay flat and high no matter how short the actual question is

Cached: turn one writes the 40,000-token prefix to cache (paying the write premium); turn two through N, while inside the TTL, reprocess only the 200 new tokens at the discounted cache-read rate on the 40,000
The saving grows with how many turns land inside one TTL window — one-off single-shot calls barely benefit, since they only ever pay the write price

slides.title: The Prefix Has to Match Exactly — and the Clock Is Ticking
slides.body: Prompt caching is a positional-match optimization, not a semantic one, and that makes it easy to accidentally defeat.
bullets: Any edit before the cache breakpoint — a reordered few-shot example, an injected timestamp, a different tool listed first — invalidates the cache for everything after it
Put stable content (instructions, tool defs, examples) first and volatile content (the live user turn) last, or you'll never get a hit
If traffic doesn't reuse the same prefix again before the TTL expires, you only ever pay the more expensive write price and never recoup it
Caching a prefix stuffed with per-user IDs or live data wastes the discount — cache what's actually shared across calls

slides.title: Order Your Prompt for the Cache, Then Measure It
slides.body: Prompt caching turns per-call cost from O(total prompt length) into roughly O(new tokens) — but only for prefixes that are stable and actually get reused.
bullets: Structure prompts static-first, dynamic-last: system prompt → tools → few-shot examples → (cache breakpoint) → live conversation
Track cache hit rate as a first-class metric alongside latency and cost — a low hit rate usually means something upstream keeps changing the prefix
It's a free win for high-volume agents and chat apps with a large shared context; it's close to useless for single, one-off completions

questions.prompt: What determines whether a prompt-caching cache hit occurs on a new request?
options: The new prompt has similar meaning to a previous one
The new prompt's prefix matches a previously cached prefix exactly, token-for-token, from the start
The request uses the same API key as before
The model's temperature setting is unchanged
questions.explanation: Caching is a positional, exact-match optimization on the token sequence — not a semantic one. Editing anything before the cache breakpoint, even a timestamp, invalidates the cache for every token after it.

questions.prompt: Why does prompt caching mainly pay off for high-volume agents with a large shared prefix, rather than one-off single questions?
options: Caching is technically disabled for short prompts
The first call pays a premium to write the cache, so only repeated reuse of that prefix within the TTL earns the discount back
Cache reads are billed at full price regardless of hits
One-off questions aren't allowed to use cached prefixes at all
questions.explanation: A cache write typically costs more than a normal input token. A single call that never gets reused only ever pays that premium — the savings only materialize once later calls hit the cache within its TTL.

questions.prompt: You have a 40K-token system prompt and want to maximize cache hits across turns. Where should the volatile, per-turn user message go relative to the cache breakpoint?
options: Before the stable content, so it's processed first
Interleaved throughout the stable content for balance
After the stable content and the cache breakpoint, since anything before the breakpoint must stay identical
It doesn't matter where it goes
questions.explanation: Because the match is positional and exact, only content before the cache breakpoint needs to stay identical across calls. Put static content (system prompt, tools, examples) first, and the changing user turn last.

posts.title: Activity Frames: Replay a Task Instead of Re-Deriving It
posts.subtitle: A deterministic compiler turns a day of screen activity into workflows an agent can run at near-zero token cost
posts.summary: Activity Frames compiles raw screen recordings into deterministic, agent-executable 'frames' instead of feeding raw pixels to an LLM. Computer-use agents stop re-deriving the same repetitive task from scratch and instead replay a compiled workflow, cutting token cost on the happy path to near zero.

slides.title: Your agent forgets what you did five minutes ago
slides.body: Every new conversation with a computer-use agent starts blind — it doesn't know what you already did today, and it re-reasons through tasks it has already solved dozens of times.

slides.title: Two failures, one root cause: no persistent activity record
slides.body: Computer-use agents burn tokens re-deriving repetitive tasks from scratch, and they start every session with zero awareness of what the user did between conversations.
bullets: Repetitive tasks (same LinkedIn outreach, same weekly report) get fully re-reasoned every single time
Agents have no grounded record of prior screen activity — no memory of apps used, sites visited, or steps taken
Feeding raw screen video to an LLM for this is expensive and non-deterministic

slides.title: A three-stage, deterministic pipeline — no LLM in the loop
slides.body: Capture, Compilation, and Serving are cleanly separated, and the compiler stage is 100% deterministic: same input always produces the same frame.
bullets: Capture: screen snapshots + accessibility-tree data + input events stream into local SQLite storage
Compilation: sessionizes activity, detects dwell periods and gaps, merges flicker, types entities via 25+ site parsers — using on-device OCR only, no remote model calls
Serving: an MCP server exposes six tools — get_context, get_activity, get_steps, get_day_summary, get_patterns, get_communications

slides.title: Tier 1 facts vs. Tier 2 inference — a hard contract
slides.body: Every frame enforces a two-tier honesty contract so an agent never mistakes a guess for a fact.
bullets: Tier 1: only measurable, deterministically-derived facts — app name, site, timestamps, duration, click/key counts
Tier 2 (optional): any inferred label gets tagged with an explicit confidence level, never presented as ground truth
Every frame keeps evidence pointers back to the raw capture rows it was built from

slides.title: Worked example: a LinkedIn outreach message, replayed not re-reasoned
slides.body: A messaging workflow performed once becomes a reusable, executable script.
bullets: The compiler reduces the demonstrated task to ordered operations — focus, click, type — grounded by element name and role
Next time, the agent slots in a new recipient and new message text, then replays the script instead of re-deriving the steps
Roughly 342 minutes of a day's raw activity compresses to about 150 words of context — and a full day compiles in under one second

slides.title: Re-deriving vs. replaying a known task
slides.body: The paper's core metric, Routine Overhead Ratio, measures exactly this gap across weeks of real activity.

rows: Under 1 second for a full day

slides.title: Where it breaks down
slides.body: This only helps with tasks the user has already performed — and it trades some setup complexity for that speedup.
bullets: Genuinely novel, first-time tasks have no prior frame to replay — the agent is back to full reasoning
Unknown or unlisted websites fall back to generic references instead of rich, typed entities (25+ sites get full parsing, the long tail doesn't)
Local-only by design: typed text capture is opt-in (--include-text) and audio is off by default, so some workflows need explicit consent flags
v0.2, tested primarily on Apple Silicon macOS — the Intel build exists but is less exercised

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Deterministic compilation, not another model call, is what makes agent memory cheap and trustworthy.
bullets: Separating capture, deterministic compilation, and MCP serving keeps the expensive part (LLM reasoning) out of the memory pipeline entirely
The Tier 1 / Tier 2 fact-vs-inference split is a reusable pattern for any agent memory system that wants to avoid hallucinated context
Replay only pays off for repeated work — pair it with normal reasoning for anything the user hasn't done before

questions.prompt: What is the main problem Activity Frames is designed to solve?
options: Slow screen recording performance on older hardware
Agents re-deriving repetitive tasks from scratch and lacking a record of what the user already did
LLMs being unable to read accessibility trees
A lack of open-source screen recording software
questions.explanation: The paper targets two linked failures: agents burning tokens re-reasoning through tasks they've already performed, and agents starting each session blind to prior user activity.

questions.prompt: Why does the compilation stage use no LLM calls?
options: LLMs are too slow to run locally
To keep compilation deterministic and cheap — the same capture data always produces the same frame
Because the accessibility tree cannot be read by language models
To comply with app store policies
questions.explanation: Compilation relies on on-device OCR and rule-based sessionizing/entity-typing instead of a model, so the same input reliably produces the same output — a property replay depends on.

questions.prompt: What does the Tier 1 / Tier 2 distinction protect against?
options: Running out of disk space
Presenting an inferred or guessed label as if it were a measured fact
Exceeding the MCP server's rate limit
Losing data if the recording app crashes
questions.explanation: Tier 1 holds only directly measurable facts (timestamps, click counts, app names); Tier 2 holds inferences, always tagged with a confidence level, so downstream agents can tell a fact from a guess.

posts.title: Chunking Strategies: The RAG Decision Nobody Profiles
posts.subtitle: How you split a document decides what your retriever can ever find — before the embedding model gets a vote
posts.summary: Chunking — how a document gets split before embedding — sets a hard ceiling on retrieval quality that no downstream model can fix. Fixed-size, structure-aware, semantic, and sentence-window chunking each trade off simplicity, coherence, and ingest cost differently, and picking wrong shows up as silent recall failures, not errors.

slides.title: The retrieval bug that never throws an exception
slides.body: Teams tune embedding models and rerankers for weeks while the actual ceiling on recall was set at ingest time, by how the document got cut into pieces.

slides.title: Fixed-size chunking splits ideas, not just text
slides.body: The simplest approach — cut every N tokens — has no idea where a sentence, clause, or table row actually ends.
bullets: A 512-token window can cut a clause defining a term in half, embedding neither half well
The query 'what is the termination clause' can score low against both halves even though the answer is right there
Recall failures like this are silent: no error, no crash, just a document the retriever should have found and didn't

slides.title: Four common strategies, in order of complexity
slides.body: Each strategy moves the tradeoff between simplicity and semantic coherence.
bullets: Fixed-size + overlap: split every N tokens (commonly 256–512) with ~10–20% overlap so boundary content appears in two chunks
Recursive / structure-aware: split on markdown headers, paragraphs, or sentence boundaries first, falling back to fixed-size only when a section is still too large
Semantic chunking: embed sentences, then cut where consecutive-sentence similarity drops — chunks track topic shifts instead of a token count
Sentence-window retrieval: index single sentences for precise matching, but return a wider window of surrounding text as the actual context

slides.title: Worked example: a 40-page vendor contract
slides.body: The same document, chunked three ways, produces three very different retrieval outcomes for one query.
bullets: Fixed-size (512 tokens, 50-token overlap): the 'Effective Date' clause spans a chunk boundary — a query for it retrieves the wrong half more than a third of the time
Structure-aware (split on section headers like '§4 Termination'): the clause stays intact, retrieval recall jumps because the chunk is exactly the semantic unit a lawyer would also read
Semantic chunking: correctly isolates the clause too, but costs an extra embedding pass over every sentence at ingest time before chunk boundaries are even decided

slides.title: Picking a strategy
slides.body: No single method wins on every axis — pick based on document structure and ingest budget.

rows: Docs with real headings (contracts, docs, wikis)
Dense prose with no clear structure
More moving parts in the pipeline

slides.title: Pitfalls and when to stop tuning this
slides.body: Chunking has diminishing returns past a point, and overlap isn't free.
bullets: Chunks too small (under ~100 tokens): high retrieval noise, and the embedding carries too little context to be distinctive
Chunks too large (over ~1–2k tokens): the query's signal gets diluted by unrelated content in the same chunk, hurting cosine similarity
Overlap multiplies storage and can return near-duplicate chunks in the same result set — dedup downstream or it wastes context budget
If the source is already structured data (a database table, a key-value config), don't chunk it at all — query it directly instead of forcing it through embeddings

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Chunking is a retrieval-quality decision, not a preprocessing detail — treat it with the same rigor as choosing an embedding model.
bullets: Default to structure-aware chunking whenever the source has real headings or sections — it's usually free recall improvement over fixed-size
Reach for semantic chunking only when the ingest cost is worth it — dense, unstructured prose with no natural breakpoints
Always keep some overlap (10–20%) so boundary-spanning facts survive in at least one chunk
Measure recall on real queries before and after a chunking change — it's the cheapest lever in a RAG pipeline and the easiest to get wrong silently

questions.prompt: Why can fixed-size chunking cause a retriever to miss an obviously relevant passage?
options: The embedding model doesn't support long documents
It can split a semantic unit (like a clause or sentence) across two chunks, weakening both embeddings
Fixed-size chunks are always too large to embed
Vector databases reject fixed-size chunks
questions.explanation: Fixed-size chunking ignores content structure, so it can cut a sentence or clause in half — neither resulting chunk embeds the full idea well, which lowers similarity to a relevant query.

questions.prompt: What does semantic chunking use to decide where to cut a document?
options: A fixed token count only
Random sampling of paragraphs
Drops in similarity between consecutive sentence embeddings
The file size in kilobytes
questions.explanation: Semantic chunking embeds sentences and cuts where consecutive-sentence similarity drops sharply, aligning chunk boundaries with actual topic shifts rather than a token count.

questions.prompt: When should you skip chunking and embeddings entirely?
options: When the document is longer than 10 pages
When the source is already structured data, like a database table, that can be queried directly
When the embedding model is expensive
Chunking should never be skipped for RAG
questions.explanation: Structured data like database tables or key-value configs can be queried exactly — forcing it through chunking and embeddings adds cost and imprecision for no benefit.

posts.title: LLM-as-a-Judge: Using One Model to Grade Another's Answers
posts.subtitle: Human eval doesn't scale past a few hundred examples — a well-prompted judge model can grade thousands, if you guard against its blind spots.
posts.summary: LLM-as-a-judge uses a capable model, prompted with a rubric, to score or compare another model's outputs — turning evaluation from a slow human bottleneck into something that runs on every commit. It comes in pointwise, pairwise, and reference-graded flavors, each with different consistency and cost tradeoffs, but every flavor inherits its own blind spots: position bias, verbosity bias, and self-preference bias.

slides.title: Grading at Scale: Let a Model Be the Judge
slides.body: LLM-as-a-judge uses a capable model, prompted with a rubric, to score or compare another model's outputs — turning evaluation from a slow human bottleneck into something you can run on every commit.

slides.title: Human Evaluation Doesn't Scale With Iteration Speed
bullets: A team shipping model or prompt changes weekly can't wait days for human annotators to score a few hundred outputs on helpfulness, tone, and accuracy
Automatic metrics like BLEU or ROUGE compare token overlap, not meaning — they reward a paraphrase of the wrong answer and penalize a correct one phrased differently
Without fast, reliable scoring, teams either ship blind or bottleneck every change behind a human review queue

slides.title: The Judge Prompt: Rubric In, Verdict Out
slides.body: A judge call is just another LLM call: system prompt with grading criteria, the candidate output (or two outputs to compare), and a required output format.
bullets: Pointwise grading: the judge scores one response alone against a rubric (e.g. 1-10 on helpfulness, factuality, tone) — cheap, but scores can drift across different grading sessions
Pairwise grading: the judge sees two responses side by side and picks A, B, or tie — more consistent than pointwise because it's a relative, not absolute, judgment
Reference-graded: the judge also gets a known-correct answer or rubric example to compare against, which sharply reduces ambiguity for factual tasks
The judge model should usually be stronger than (or at least a different family from) the models it's grading, to reduce blind spots they might share

slides.title: Why Pairwise Beats Pointwise for Consistency
slides.body: Asking 'is this an 8 or a 9' forces the judge to hold an internal absolute scale steady across hundreds of independent calls — that scale drifts. Asking 'which of these two is better' only requires a stable ordering, which LLMs do more reliably.
bullets: Pairwise comparisons compose into a ranking (via win-rate or an Elo-style update), which is exactly how large-scale human-preference leaderboards work
Cost tradeoff: ranking n candidates by pairwise comparison needs many more judge calls than pointwise scoring — fine for picking a best-of-k, expensive for grading a large static eval set
Most production eval pipelines use pointwise for regression tracking over time (needs an absolute scale to compare week over week) and pairwise for picking a winner between two specific candidates

slides.title: Three Grading Modes, Three Use Cases

rows: Picking a winner, A/B testing prompts
Factual QA, coding tasks with ground truth

slides.title: Worked Example: Grading a Support Agent's Reply
slides.body: A prompt engineer changes the system prompt for a support bot and needs to know if replies actually got better.
bullets: Judge prompt: 'Given this customer message and the agent's reply, score 1-5 on: (1) directly answers the question, (2) matches company tone, (3) doesn't invent policy details. Output JSON: {scores: [...], reasoning: ...}.'
Run both the old and new prompt's replies through the same judge on 200 held-out customer messages

The new prompt averages higher on 'answers the question' than the old — a real signal, but the judge's reasoning also flags that the new prompt occasionally invents a refund policy that doesn't exist, which the aggregate score alone would have hidden
Lesson: always spot-check the judge's written reasoning, not just its numeric score — the reasoning surfaces failure modes the number smooths over

slides.title: Where the Judge Itself Gets Fooled
bullets: Position bias: in pairwise grading, judges tend to favor whichever answer is shown first — mitigate by grading each pair twice with the order swapped and checking for agreement
Verbosity bias: judges systematically rate longer answers as better even when they're not more correct, so a rubric that doesn't explicitly penalize padding gets gamed by it
Self-preference bias: a judge model tends to rate outputs written in its own family's style more favorably, which inflates scores when the same model family both generates and grades
A judge is not a substitute for held-out human spot-checks on a sample — treat judge scores as a fast, noisy first pass, not ground truth

slides.title: When to Reach for an LLM Judge
bullets: Use it for fast iteration signal — regression tracking, prompt A/B tests, filtering large generation sets down to a human-reviewable shortlist
Always randomize/swap presentation order in pairwise setups and read a sample of the judge's reasoning, not just the score
Don't use it as the sole gate for anything high-stakes (safety, compliance, medical/legal content) — keep a human in the loop there
Prefer a judge from a different model family than the one being graded, and re-validate the judge's agreement with humans on a small labeled sample before trusting it at scale

questions.prompt: What's the main reason pairwise grading tends to be more consistent than pointwise grading?
options: Pairwise grading is always cheaper to run
Pairwise only requires a stable relative ordering, not a fixed absolute scale held steady across many calls
Pairwise grading doesn't require a rubric
Pointwise grading can only be used with reference answers
questions.explanation: Holding an absolute score (like 'is this an 8 or a 9') steady across hundreds of separate judge calls is harder than making one relative call ('which is better'), which is why pairwise comparisons tend to be more internally consistent.

questions.prompt: A team uses the same model family to both generate responses and judge them, and notices judge scores are unusually high. What bias does this most likely illustrate?
options: Position bias
Verbosity bias
Self-preference bias
Reference bias
questions.explanation: Self-preference bias is when a judge model rates outputs written in a style similar to its own family more favorably — a known reason to prefer a judge from a different model family than the one it's grading.

questions.prompt: Why should you read a judge model's written reasoning, not just its numeric score?
options: The numeric score is always randomly generated
Reasoning is required by the schema and has no other purpose
The reasoning can surface specific failure modes (like an invented policy detail) that an aggregate score alone would hide
Numeric scores are never comparable across different judge calls
questions.explanation: In the worked example, the new prompt scored higher on average but the judge's reasoning revealed it occasionally invented a refund policy — a real regression the aggregate number alone wouldn't have surfaced.

posts.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: Merging Keyword and Vector Search Without Retraining Anything
posts.subtitle: Two ranked lists disagree — RRF trusts whichever document shows up strong in both, using nothing but rank position.
posts.summary: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) merges results from different retrievers — like BM25 keyword search and a vector index — into one ranked list using only each document's rank position, never its raw score. That sidesteps the problem of comparing an unbounded BM25 score to a bounded cosine similarity, needs no training or tuning, and is the standard default for hybrid search in modern RAG pipelines.

slides.title: One Query, Two Rankers, One List
slides.body: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combines a keyword search's ranking and a vector search's ranking into a single ordering — using only each document's rank position, never its raw score.

slides.title: Keyword Search and Vector Search Fail in Opposite Ways
bullets: BM25 keyword search nails exact terms — SKUs, error codes, proper nouns — but misses a query phrased differently than the document ('laptop won't turn on' vs. a doc that says 'device fails to power up')

Dense vector search catches that paraphrase because it matches meaning, but can bury a document containing the literal rare token the user typed, since embeddings smooth rare tokens into a general semantic neighborhood
Picking one system as your only retriever means picking one of these failure modes on every single query

slides.title: Fuse by Rank, Not by Score
slides.body: The obvious fix — average the two systems' raw scores — breaks immediately: BM25 scores are unbounded term-frequency statistics, cosine similarity is bounded in [-1,1], and neither is calibrated against the other.
bullets: RRF sidesteps calibration entirely: for each ranked list, keep each document's rank position (1st, 2nd, 3rd…) and throw the raw score away
Formula: RRF(d) = Σ 1 / (k + rank_r(d)) — summed over every ranked list r that contains document d
k is a small constant that dampens how much a #1 spot dominates a #10 spot; the original 2009 paper and most implementations (including Elasticsearch's default) use k=60
A document that never appears in a given list simply contributes 0 from that list — no penalty term needed

slides.title: Why Rank Beats Score Here
slides.body: Rank position is already a comparable, unit-free number across any retriever — a BM25 rank of 3 and a vector rank of 3 mean the same thing ('third-best'), even though a BM25 score of 3 and a cosine score of 3 mean nothing comparable.
bullets: This makes RRF a drop-in fusion for any pair (or trio+) of rankers — swap BM25 for SPLADE, or add a third reranked list — with zero retuning
The 1/(k+rank) shape is deliberately convex: moving from rank 1→2 costs more than moving from rank 20→21, so agreement near the top of the lists matters most
No training, no learned weights — it's a fixed formula applied at query time, unlike learned fusion methods that need labeled query-document pairs

slides.title: Worked Example: Fusing Two 5-Item Lists (k=60)
slides.body: A query returns these two ranked lists of document IDs:
bullets: BM25 order: D3, D1, D7, D2, D5 → D1 sits at rank 2, contributing 1/62 ≈ 0.0161
Vector order: D1, D2, D9, D3, D6 → D1 sits at rank 1, contributing 1/61 ≈ 0.0164
D1's total RRF score: 0.0161 + 0.0164 ≈ 0.0325 — the highest of any document in the fused list
D3 was BM25's #1 pick (1/61 ≈ 0.0164) but only rank 4 in vector search (1/64 ≈ 0.0156), totaling ≈0.0320 — just enough to lose the top spot to D1, which was strong (though not #1) in BOTH lists

slides.title: What Each Retriever Alone Misses

rows: Just sum in a third ranked list

slides.title: Where RRF Falls Short
bullets: It only ever reorders documents that at least one retriever already surfaced — if both BM25 and vector search miss a relevant doc entirely, RRF can't recover it
The constant k is a blunt global knob; it doesn't adapt per query, even when one retriever is obviously more trustworthy for that specific query
It ignores confidence magnitude — a retriever that's barely sure about its #1 result counts exactly as much as one that's very sure, since only rank position is used

It's not a substitute for a cross-encoder reranker: RRF is a cheap way to merge candidate lists, but a reranker that reads query and document together usually beats RRF-only ordering on the final top-k

slides.title: When to Reach for RRF
bullets: Default choice for combining BM25 and vector search in a RAG pipeline — a few lines of code, no training data required, robust to differently-scaled retrievers
Use it to merge candidate lists BEFORE an expensive reranker, not as a replacement for one — RRF for cheap fusion, reranker for final precision
Tune k only if eval data shows it matters — k=60 is a reasonable default most systems never need to change
If one retriever is simply broken, RRF will still be dragged down by it — fix or drop the bad retriever rather than trying to fuse around it

questions.prompt: What does RRF actually use to combine rankings from different retrievers?
options: Each retriever's raw similarity/relevance score
Only the rank position of each document within each list
A machine-learned weight trained on labeled query-document pairs
The number of query terms each document contains
questions.explanation: RRF deliberately discards raw scores because they're not comparable across retrievers (unbounded BM25 term-frequency scores vs. bounded cosine similarity). Using only rank position sidesteps that calibration problem entirely.

questions.prompt: In RRF(d) = Σ 1/(k + rank_r(d)), what does increasing the constant k do?
options: Disqualifies documents ranked below k
Flattens the curve, reducing how much a #1 rank dominates over a lower rank
Converts vector search into keyword search
Requires re-training the retriever
questions.explanation: A larger k shrinks the relative gap between 1/(k+1) and 1/(k+10), so top ranks matter less relative to lower ones. Most systems use k=60 as a default that avoids letting the #1 slot completely dominate the fused score.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, why did D1 (rank 2 in BM25, rank 1 in vector) outrank D3 (rank 1 in BM25, rank 4 in vector)?
options: D1 had a higher raw BM25 score
RRF always prefers whichever document is #1 in the vector list
D1's summed rank-based score across both lists was higher — being strong in both beat being #1 in only one
D3 was excluded for not appearing in enough lists
questions.explanation: RRF sums each list's contribution. D1's two solid-but-not-top ranks (2nd and 1st) summed to a higher score than D3's single #1 rank plus a mediocre 4th-place rank elsewhere — exactly the behavior that makes fusion valuable: a consistent runner-up can beat a list's top pick.

posts.title: Knowledge Distillation: Training a Small Model to Copy a Big One
posts.subtitle: The teacher doesn't hand over its weights — it hands over its uncertainty, and that's the part that actually teaches.
posts.summary: Knowledge distillation trains a small 'student' model to match a large 'teacher' model's full probability distribution, not just its final answer — because the relative probabilities the teacher assigns to wrong answers carry information a hard label throws away. Done well, a student can keep most of the teacher's quality at a fraction of the size and latency.

slides.title: You Don't Need the Whole Brain — You Need What It Knows
slides.body: Knowledge distillation compresses a large, expensive model into a small, cheap one by training the small model to imitate the large one's behavior, not just its labels.

slides.title: The Big Model Is Accurate and Unaffordable
bullets: A frontier-scale model gives the best answers, but every request costs real GPU-seconds and real dollars
Edge devices, latency-sensitive endpoints, and high-QPS services often can't fit or afford the teacher at all
Training a small model from scratch on the same data usually lands well below the big model's accuracy — the small model needs more than raw labels to close the gap

slides.title: Train the Student on the Teacher's Soft Labels
slides.body: Instead of only training the student on the correct answer (a 'hard label'), distillation also trains it to match the teacher's full output distribution over all possible answers (a 'soft label').
bullets: Run the teacher on the training data and keep its output probabilities, not just its top prediction
Train the student with a loss that combines: (1) normal cross-entropy against the true label, and (2) a term pulling the student's distribution toward the teacher's distribution
The student never needs the teacher again at serving time — only during training

slides.title: Why Soft Labels Work: 'Dark Knowledge'
slides.body: A temperature parameter softens the teacher's distribution so the small probabilities on wrong answers become visible instead of rounding to zero.
bullets: Example: for an image of a wolf, a hard label says 100% 'wolf'. A teacher's soft label might say 90% wolf, 9% husky, 1% cat — that 9% tells the student wolves and huskies look alike, information a hard label discards entirely
Raising the softmax temperature spreads out the distribution further, exposing more of these relative similarities during training
Hinton, Vinyals & Dean (2015) named this extra signal 'dark knowledge' — it's why a distilled student generalizes better than one trained on hard labels alone

slides.title: A Well-Known Result: DistilBERT
slides.body: Distilling BERT-base into a 6-layer student (Sanh et al., 2019) is one of the most-cited demonstrations that this tradeoff can be very favorable.
bullets: Measured on the GLUE benchmark suite against the full BERT-base teacher
The gap wasn't zero — but it was small relative to the size and speed win

slides.title: Worked Example: Shrinking a Support Chatbot
slides.body: A team runs a customer-support assistant on a large frontier model and needs to cut latency and cost for a high-volume tier-1 triage flow.
bullets: They log thousands of real (query, teacher-response, teacher-confidence) triples from production traffic
A much smaller model is trained to match the teacher's response distribution on that logged traffic, not just to copy the final text
The small model handles the high-volume, well-covered cases at a fraction of the cost; anything the student is uncertain about still escalates to the big model
Result: most traffic gets cheap, fast answers, while quality on the hard tail doesn't regress

slides.title: Where Distillation Falls Short
bullets: A student can't exceed what the teacher knows — distillation transfers behavior, it doesn't add new capability
The student inherits the teacher's blind spots and biases along with its skill
It's not free: you still need the teacher available for inference during training, and building a good distillation dataset takes real engineering

Different from quantization: quantization keeps the same architecture and shrinks numeric precision; distillation trains a genuinely smaller architecture from scratch — the two are often combined, not substitutes for each other

slides.title: When to Reach for Distillation
bullets: Use it when you have a strong teacher and a narrower, well-defined task the student needs to cover — general-purpose 'shrink everything' distillation is much harder
The win comes from soft labels carrying relative-probability information, not just from having more training data
Pair with quantization and pruning for compounding gains — they attack different bottlenecks
Budget real evaluation on your target task; a student that matches GLUE-style benchmarks can still regress on your specific long-tail queries

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between training a student on 'hard labels' versus the teacher's 'soft labels'?
options: Hard labels are faster to compute; soft labels require no teacher at all
Soft labels are the teacher's full probability distribution over all answers, which carries information about which wrong answers are 'almost right'
Soft labels only apply to image models, not language models
There is no real difference — it's just different terminology for the same thing
questions.explanation: A hard label collapses to one correct answer with 100% probability. A soft label keeps the teacher's probabilities across all answers, so the student also learns which wrong answers the teacher considered plausible — the 'dark knowledge' that improves generalization.

questions.prompt: What does raising the softmax temperature do during distillation?
options: It makes the teacher model run faster
It spreads out the probability distribution, making small probabilities on non-top answers more visible to the student
It reduces the size of the student model
It converts soft labels back into hard labels
questions.explanation: A higher temperature softens (flattens) the softmax output, so probabilities on the teacher's less-likely answers stop rounding to near-zero and become usable training signal.

questions.prompt: How does knowledge distillation differ from quantization?
options: They are the same technique with different names
Quantization reduces numeric precision on the same architecture; distillation trains a smaller architecture to imitate a teacher's behavior — they're often combined
Distillation only works on the exact same model size as the teacher
Quantization requires a teacher model and distillation does not
questions.explanation: Quantization keeps the same parameter count but stores/computes with lower precision. Distillation actually trains a smaller model from scratch to mimic a larger one's outputs. Both reduce cost, but by attacking different bottlenecks, so they compose well together.

posts.title: Reflexion: An Agent That Critiques Its Own Attempts
posts.subtitle: No gradient updates — just a verbal self-critique stored in memory and replayed next try
posts.summary: Reflexion is a pattern where an agent that fails a task doesn't retrain — it writes itself a short critique of what went wrong and carries that note into its next attempt. An actor generates the trajectory, an evaluator scores it, and a self-reflection step turns the score into language that becomes part of the next prompt. It's cheap, fast, and works within a single session, but it has real limits: it needs a trustworthy pass/fail signal, and the reflections themselves can be wrong.

slides.title: An agent that grades its own homework — and remembers the grade
slides.body: Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) lets a language agent improve across attempts at the same task without touching a single weight — it just writes itself a better prompt for next time.

slides.title: A plain retry loop fails the same way twice
bullets: A basic agent (e.g. ReAct) that fails a task and just tries again has no memory of *why* it failed — it's re-rolling the dice, not fixing anything
Fine-tuning or RL after every failure is too slow and too expensive to run inside a single user session
Most agent failures are 'near misses' — one wrong assumption, one skipped edge case — not fundamental capability gaps that need retraining

slides.title: Three roles share one growing transcript
slides.body: Reflexion splits the loop into three jobs played by the same or different LLM calls: an Actor that acts, an Evaluator that scores the outcome, and a Self-Reflection step that turns the score into a lesson.
bullets: Actor: attempts the task and produces a trajectory of actions/outputs
Evaluator: scores the trajectory against a task signal — unit tests passing, an environment reward, or an LLM-as-judge verdict
Self-reflection model: reads the trajectory + score and writes a short natural-language critique of what to do differently
That critique is appended to an episodic memory buffer and included in the prompt for the next attempt — the 'learning' lives in context, not in weights

slides.title: The loop runs until it succeeds or the budget runs out
slides.body: Each trial is: act → evaluate → reflect → retry, with the memory buffer growing by one entry per failed trial.
bullets: The buffer is usually capped at the last few reflections — unbounded growth just burns context window for no extra benefit
Stopping conditions: the evaluator reports success, or a max-trial budget (commonly single digits) is hit
Because reflection is just text, it's model-agnostic and needs zero training infrastructure — it's a prompting and memory pattern, not an architecture change

slides.title: Worked example: a failing coding attempt
slides.body: Task: write a function that returns the sum of a list, handling empty input.
bullets: Attempt 1: agent submits code that crashes on an empty list — evaluator runs the unit tests and reports 2/5 failing
Self-reflection: "The function assumes the list is non-empty and divides by len(list); add a guard for the empty case and return 0."
That sentence is prepended to the next attempt's prompt as memory
Attempt 2: agent adds the guard clause first, before touching the rest of the logic — evaluator reports 5/5 passing

slides.title: Reflexion sits between dumb retries and full fine-tuning

rows: One extra LLM call per trial
Only if memory is saved externally

slides.title: Where it breaks down
bullets: Garbage evaluator, garbage reflection: if the pass/fail signal is noisy or gameable, the agent learns a confidently wrong lesson and repeats it
The self-reflection step can misdiagnose the actual bug — a plausible-sounding critique isn't guaranteed to be the correct one
Reflections are episodic by default — close the session and the 'learning' is gone unless you persist the memory buffer yourself
Diminishing returns: most of the gain shows up in the first 2-3 trials; grinding more attempts mostly just adds context-window cost

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Reflexion = Actor + Evaluator + Self-reflection, looped, with critiques stored as text in memory instead of gradients in weights
It's the cheapest way to let an agent improve within a session — no training run required
It only works as well as its evaluator; without a trustworthy success/failure signal, don't bother
Treat it as a few-trial boost, not a replacement for fine-tuning when you need the improvement to persist or generalize

questions.prompt: What does Reflexion update after a failed attempt?
options: The model's weights, via a gradient step
A verbal self-critique stored in an episodic memory buffer
The evaluator's reward function
The sampling temperature
questions.explanation: Reflexion never touches weights. The self-reflection step writes a natural-language critique that gets replayed as context on the next attempt — the improvement lives in the prompt, not the parameters.

questions.prompt: Which component decides whether an attempt actually succeeded or failed?
options: The actor
The self-reflection model
The evaluator
The episodic memory buffer
questions.explanation: The evaluator supplies the ground-truth-ish signal — unit tests, an environment reward, or an LLM judge — that decides whether the loop stops or a reflection gets written.

questions.prompt: What's a real risk of running many Reflexion trials back to back?
options: It requires more GPUs because each trial needs backpropagation
The growing reflection history eats context window, and a wrong self-diagnosis can get entrenched across trials
It always converges to 100% success after enough trials
It stops functioning after exactly one trial by design
questions.explanation: There's no backprop involved, so GPU cost isn't the issue. The real risks are context-window bloat from an ever-growing memory buffer and a confidently wrong self-critique compounding across attempts.

posts.title: DPO: Skipping the Reward Model Entirely
posts.subtitle: How Direct Preference Optimization turned RLHF into a single supervised loss
posts.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) collapses RLHF's three-stage pipeline — supervised fine-tuning, reward model training, and PPO — into one supervised classification loss trained directly on (chosen, rejected) pairs. It's simpler and more stable than PPO-based RLHF, but it has its own failure modes worth knowing before you reach for it.

slides.title: One loss function replaces an entire RL pipeline
slides.body: DPO (2023) showed you can align a language model to human preferences without ever training a reward model or running PPO — just supervised learning on pairs of responses.

slides.title: Classic RLHF is three fragile stages stacked together
bullets: Stage 1: supervised fine-tune (SFT) on demonstrations
Stage 2: train a separate reward model on human preference pairs
Stage 3: run PPO to optimize the policy against that reward model — an RL loop notorious for instability, reward hacking, and finicky hyperparameters
Each stage needs its own infra, and errors in the reward model propagate straight into the RL objective

slides.title: Reparameterize the reward model out of the objective
slides.body: DPO's key insight: the RLHF objective (maximize reward, minus a KL penalty from a reference model) has a closed-form optimal policy. Invert that relationship and the 'reward' is just a function of the policy's own log-probabilities — so you can write a loss directly on preference pairs and skip fitting a reward model at all.
bullets: Needs only a policy model + a frozen reference model (usually the SFT checkpoint)
Trains with plain supervised cross-entropy-style loss on (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples
No sampling, no reward model, no PPO — a single training stage after SFT

slides.title: The loss pushes apart log-prob ratios, not raw scores
slides.body: For each pair, DPO compares how much more (or less) likely the policy makes the chosen response vs. the rejected one, relative to the same gap under the frozen reference model.
bullets: Loss = -log σ(β · [log-ratio(chosen) − log-ratio(rejected)])
β controls how far the policy is allowed to drift from the reference — small β stays conservative, large β can overfit preferences and degrade general ability
Because the reference model appears in the loss, it acts as an implicit regularizer — no separate KL penalty term to tune

slides.title: DPO trades RL complexity for data sensitivity

rows: Likelihood displacement, sensitive to label noise

slides.title: Worked example: teaching a chatbot to stop rambling
slides.body: You have pairs like (prompt: 'What's a hash map?', chosen: a tight 3-sentence answer, rejected: a rambling 3-paragraph one). During training, DPO increases the model's relative log-probability of the concise answer and decreases it for the rambling one — always measured relative to what the frozen reference model would have assigned.
bullets: After enough pairs, the policy shifts its whole distribution toward the 'concise' style without ever being told explicitly 'be concise'
No reward score is computed anywhere — the preference signal flows straight into gradient updates

slides.title: Where DPO breaks down — and when to avoid it
bullets: Likelihood displacement: DPO can lower the probability of BOTH responses in a pair — it only needs the chosen one to drop less, which can leak probability mass onto unrelated, sometimes worse completions
No online exploration: unlike PPO, DPO only ever sees the fixed pairs you gave it, so it can't discover or correct for failure modes outside that dataset
Sensitive to label noise: with no reward model smoothing disagreement across many samples, a single mislabeled pair has an outsized effect
Avoid it when you need iterative, on-policy refinement against a live reward signal, or when your preference data is noisy and unvetted

slides.title: Why DPO won post-training in the open-weight world
bullets: One supervised loss instead of an RL loop — cheaper, more stable, easier to debug
Became the default post-training step for many open-weight model families after SFT
Its known weaknesses (likelihood displacement, offline-only) spawned follow-up variants like IPO, KTO, and ORPO that patch specific failure modes
Rule of thumb: reach for DPO when you have clean preference pairs and want simple, stable alignment; reach for online RL when you need the model to keep exploring against a live reward

questions.prompt: What does DPO eliminate compared to classic PPO-based RLHF?
options: The separate reward model and the RL optimization loop
The need for any preference data at all
The supervised fine-tuning stage
The need for a frozen reference model
questions.explanation: DPO reparameterizes the RLHF objective so the optimal policy's implicit reward is just a function of its own log-probabilities. That lets it train directly on preference pairs with a supervised loss — no separate reward model, no PPO rollouts.

questions.prompt: In the DPO loss, what does the β hyperparameter control?
options: The learning rate schedule
How far the trained policy is allowed to drift from the reference model
The batch size used for each preference pair
The sampling temperature at inference time
questions.explanation: β scales the log-ratio gap between chosen and rejected responses, which plays the same role the KL penalty plays in PPO-based RLHF — it's an implicit regularizer pulling the policy back toward the reference model.

questions.prompt: What is 'likelihood displacement,' a known DPO failure mode?
options: The model refuses to generate any output
Training diverges and loss goes to infinity
The model can lower the probability of both the chosen and rejected response, as long as the chosen one drops less
The reference model's weights get overwritten during training
questions.explanation: Because DPO's loss only cares about the relative gap between chosen and rejected log-probabilities, it can satisfy that objective by pushing down both responses' probabilities — leaking probability mass onto other, sometimes unrelated or worse completions.

references.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model (Rafailov et al., 2023)

posts.title: Orchestrator-Worker: Splitting One Task Across Many Agents
posts.subtitle: A lead agent that delegates instead of doing everything itself trades one clean thread for raw parallel throughput — and a much bigger token bill.
posts.summary: Orchestrator-worker splits a broad task into independent subtasks that run as isolated agents in parallel, each with a clean context, then synthesizes their results into one answer. It trades a single agent's simplicity for real throughput — at the cost of more tokens, coordination overhead, and no shared state between workers.

slides.title: What If One Agent Delegated Instead of Doing Everything Itself?
slides.body: A single agent chews through a long task one step at a time, on one thread, inside one context window. The orchestrator-worker pattern breaks that open: a lead agent decomposes the task and hands the pieces to separate worker agents that run in parallel.

slides.title: A Single Agent Hits a Serial, Crowded-Context Ceiling
slides.body: Give one agent a broad task and every sub-question competes for the same context window and the same turn-by-turn clock.
bullets: Independent sub-tasks still run one after another inside one context window — five unrelated lookups cost five sequential round-trips, even though nothing about them actually depends on the others
Detail from sub-task #1 stays in context while the agent works on sub-task #4, crowding out the tokens that matter right now and raising the odds it loses the thread on a long task
One long-running trajectory has no natural place to fail gracefully — a wrong turn early on can quietly drag every downstream step off course with it

slides.title: An Orchestrator Decomposes, Workers Run in Isolated Parallel
slides.body: The lead agent's only job is to plan, dispatch, and synthesize — the actual digging happens in disposable worker agents.
bullets: The orchestrator reads the task once and writes out a small set of independent, clearly-scoped subtasks — each phrased so a worker can complete it without needing the others
Each subtask spins up its own worker agent with a fresh, clean context — it never sees the orchestrator's full history or any other worker's scratch work, only its one assignment
Workers run concurrently, not in sequence — wall-clock time tracks the slowest single subtask, not the sum of all of them
Each worker hands back a compact result, not its full trajectory — the orchestrator synthesizes the final answer from those summaries rather than re-reading everyone's raw work

slides.title: Single Agent vs. Orchestrator-Worker

rows: Shares one growing window with everything else
Each worker gets its own clean window
Multiplies with worker count — each pays its own fixed overhead
Orchestrator must decompose well and synthesize results
Tightly sequential tasks with shared state
Broad tasks that split into independent pieces

slides.title: Comparing Five Cloud Providers' Pricing in Parallel
slides.body: A user asks: "Compare the pricing models of five major cloud providers for a specific workload."
bullets: The orchestrator writes five subtasks, one per provider, each scoped identically so the results come back comparable
Five worker agents launch at once, each with a clean context holding only its one provider's assignment — no cross-contamination from what the others find
Each worker returns a short structured summary (unit price, free tier, notable caveat) instead of its full research trace, keeping the orchestrator's synthesis step cheap

The orchestrator merges the five summaries into one comparison — if a worker's result looks thin or contradicts another, it can dispatch a follow-up before finalizing, something a single serial agent would have to interrupt its own flow to do

slides.title: The Bill: More Tokens, Less Determinism, No Shared State
slides.body: Parallelism isn't free — it's traded for cost and coordination overhead.
bullets: Every worker re-pays the fixed cost of its own instructions and tool definitions from a blank context — fanning a task out to several workers can burn noticeably more total tokens than one agent doing the same work serially
Workers can't see each other's progress mid-flight, so overlapping or duplicate work is a real risk unless the orchestrator's decomposition keeps subtasks genuinely independent
More parallel agents means more independent sources of variance in the final answer — the orchestrator's synthesis step has to reconcile that, not just concatenate it

Skip this pattern for tasks with real sequential coupling or shared mutable state — e.g. several edits to the same file, where one worker's change would clash with another's. A single agent, or a pattern like Plan-and-Execute, fits those better than parallel workers that can't coordinate

slides.title: Delegate the Independent Parts, Keep the Coupled Parts Serial
bullets: Orchestrator-worker splits a broad task into independent subtasks, runs them as isolated agents in parallel, then synthesizes the results — trading a single clean thread for raw throughput
Each worker's fresh context is the real unlock: it stops one crowded window from accumulating irrelevant detail across unrelated subtasks
The real cost is token usage and coordination — every worker re-pays fixed overhead, and duplicate or conflicting work is possible without careful decomposition
It shines when a task cleanly splits into independent pieces; tasks with shared state or tight sequential dependencies belong on a single agent instead

questions.prompt: What is the core structural change orchestrator-worker makes compared to a single agent handling everything?
options: It removes the need for any planning step
A lead agent decomposes the task and dispatches independent subtasks to separate worker agents that run in parallel
It replaces the LLM with a fixed rules engine
It merges all subtasks into one shared context window
questions.explanation: The orchestrator's job is decomposition and synthesis; the actual work happens in isolated worker agents that don't share a context, letting independent subtasks run concurrently instead of one after another.

questions.prompt: Why does each worker agent get a fresh, clean context instead of sharing the orchestrator's full history?
options: To reduce disk usage
So irrelevant detail from other subtasks doesn't crowd it out — a worker only needs its one scoped assignment, not the full history
Because workers cannot process any context at all
To force every worker to produce an identical answer
questions.explanation: A crowded shared context is exactly the problem this pattern avoids — each worker only needs its one scoped assignment, at the cost of not being able to see what its sibling workers are doing.

questions.prompt: When should you avoid the orchestrator-worker pattern in favor of a single agent?
options: Whenever there are five or more independent subtasks
Whenever the task needs to finish quickly
When subtasks share mutable state or have a real sequential dependency between them
Never — orchestrator-worker is always the better choice
questions.explanation: Isolated parallel workers can't coordinate over shared state or a strict step order — tasks with real coupling belong on a single agent, or a pattern like Plan-and-Execute, instead.

posts.title: Beacon: Teaching a Vision Model When to Reach for a Tool
posts.subtitle: Most visual agents either call a tool every time or never learn to — Beacon's reward function teaches the difference, and picks up 6 points for it.
posts.summary: Beacon is a multimodal LLM trained with two targeted reinforcement-learning mechanisms that teach it not just to use visual tools (zoom, crop, code execution) but to recognize when a tool is actually necessary versus wasted overhead. Beacon-RL-8B ranks first on 11 of 13 open-source visual-reasoning benchmarks, beating its own base model by an average of 6.07 points — gains the paper attributes specifically to better judgment about when to act, not just more tool use.

slides.title: Beacon: Teaching a Vision Model When to Reach for a Tool
slides.body: Give a vision-language model a zoom tool and a code interpreter, and it will either ignore them or lean on them for every single question. Neither is what you want.

slides.title: Tool Access Isn't the Same as Tool Judgment
slides.body: Multimodal LLMs equipped with visual tools tend to fall into one of two failure modes, and standard RL training doesn't fix either.
bullets: Under-use: the model answers straight from a downsampled image even when small text or fine detail actually requires zooming in first, and just gets it wrong
Over-use: the model invokes a tool reflexively on every question, including trivial ones, burning latency and compute for no accuracy gain
Standard RL rewards only the final answer's correctness — it can't tell the difference between 'the tool call helped' and 'the tool call was irrelevant but the answer happened to be right anyway'

slides.title: Two Reward Mechanisms, Aimed at Judgment Not Just Accuracy
slides.body: Beacon adds two mechanisms to the RL training stage, each targeting a specific failure mode.
bullets: Necessity-Aware Adaptive Reward: shapes the reward around whether a tool call was actually necessary for that specific example, not just whether the final answer was correct — this is what teaches the model to skip tools on easy questions

Hint-Guided Capability Expansion: focuses additional training signal on the hardest problems, where the base model tends to fail without tool assistance — strengthening tool-use specifically where it matters most

The paper evaluates on two separate axes rather than one aggregate score: Mode Adaptiveness (does it correctly recognize when a tool is needed?) and Tool Effect (does invoking the tool actually improve the answer?)

slides.title: Results: Beacon-RL-8B vs. the Field
slides.body: Against other open-source multimodal models across 13 benchmarks:

rows: Avg. improvement over its own base model
Mode Adaptiveness & Tool Effect, not raw tool-call frequency

slides.title: Worked Example: One Chart, Two Different Calls
slides.body: Show the same model two questions about the same chart image.
bullets: Q1: 'Which bar is the tallest?' — answerable at a glance; a well-tuned Beacon-style model skips the zoom tool entirely and answers directly, saving a full tool round-trip

Q2: 'What's the exact value printed on the third bar's tiny axis label?' — the label is unreadable at the image's native resolution, so the model correctly triggers a zoom/crop tool call before answering
A model without Necessity-Aware Adaptive Reward tends to call the tool for both questions (over-use) or neither (under-use) — Beacon's training signal is what produces the split behavior

slides.title: Where This Doesn't Automatically Generalize
slides.body: The gains are real but scoped — worth knowing the boundaries before assuming this transfers everywhere.
bullets: This is validated on visual-reasoning benchmarks specifically; the paper doesn't claim the same reward-shaping mechanisms transfer directly to pure text-based tool-use agents

Hint-Guided Capability Expansion depends on having a good supply of genuinely hard examples where tools are actually necessary — a training set skewed toward easy questions would undercut this half of the method

It's still an RL-trained model with the usual RL costs: more expensive and slower to train than supervised fine-tuning, and the reward shaping itself is a hyperparameter that has to be tuned per task distribution

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: The bottleneck in tool-using visual agents often isn't tool access — it's judgment about when a tool is worth the cost
Beacon separates 'did the tool call happen' from 'did the tool call actually help,' and rewards the latter directly via Necessity-Aware Adaptive Reward
Hint-Guided Capability Expansion concentrates training signal on the hard cases where tools genuinely change the outcome
Result: Beacon-RL-8B leads 11 of 13 open-source benchmarks with a +6.07 point average gain, driven by better tool-use judgment rather than more tool calls

Never call tools, to save compute
Invoke tools proportionally to how necessary they are for that specific example
Randomly sample which tool to call
questions.explanation: It shapes the reward around whether the tool call was actually necessary for that example, teaching the model to skip tools on easy questions and use them on ones that genuinely require them.

posts.subtitle: Persistent background agents and a crash-safe event log — Meta's first real swing at the agentic coding market, priced to undercut it.
posts.summary: Meta launched Muse Code in beta on August 5, 2026 — a terminal-based coding agent for macOS and Linux, powered by the new Muse Spark 1.2 model. Its distinguishing idea is persistent async background agents that stay alive for the whole session plus a replay-exact, restart-safe event log, aimed at surviving long, multi-step software engineering tasks. Muse Spark 1.2 itself improves on Muse Spark 1.1's coding benchmarks, and Meta is pricing standard API access below several rivals.

slides.title: Muse Code: Meta's Terminal Coding Agent Hits macOS, Linux
slides.body: Meta's answer to the crowded field of terminal coding agents leans on one idea: background agents that don't die when the main task does.

slides.title: The Failure Mode Muse Code Targets
slides.body: Long, multi-step coding tasks — a big refactor, a multi-file migration — are exactly where agentic coding tools tend to fall apart.
bullets: A crash, a dropped connection, or a long-running step mid-task usually means restarting from scratch, losing whatever progress and context existed in memory
Sub-tasks spawned to investigate a codebase (searching, testing, validating) typically have to report back before the main agent can move on, creating unnecessary serialized waiting
Meta is entering a market where Claude Code, Codex CLI, and others are already established — the pitch has to be a real architectural difference, not just another CLI wrapper

slides.title: Persistent Background Agents + a Restart-Safe Event Log

bullets: Specialized background agents stay active for the entire session rather than spinning up per task — they carry out next steps on their own and choose when to report back to the main agent, cutting serialized waiting on multi-step work
Every model call, tool run, approval, and edit is appended to a local event log that's replay-exact and restart-safe — a crash mid-task means resuming exactly where it stopped, not restarting
Ships with default skills: /plan turns a task into an approval-gated plan, /grill stress-tests that plan before execution, /goal works toward a stated objective end-to-end
Powered by the new Muse Spark 1.2 model, with a 1-million-token context window

slides.title: Worked Scenario: A Refactor That Survives a Crash

bullets: They run /plan first — Muse Code produces an approval-gated plan instead of just starting to edit, and /grill stress-tests that plan for gaps before anything runs

Mid-migration, the terminal session drops. Because every step was appended to the local event log, Muse Code resumes from the exact last completed edit instead of re-doing (or worse, re-guessing) prior work
