posts.title: Idempotency Keys: Making It Safe to Retry a Request
posts.subtitle: A network timeout can't tell you whether your request succeeded — idempotency keys let you retry blindly anyway, without charging a card twice.
posts.summary: When a network call times out, the client genuinely cannot tell whether the server processed the request before the connection dropped. Idempotency keys solve this by attaching a unique client-generated ID to each logical operation; the server stores the result the first time it sees a key and returns that stored result — never re-executing the side effect — on every retry with the same key. It's the mechanism that makes 'just retry on failure' safe for anything with a real-world side effect, like charging a card or placing an order.

slides.title: Idempotency Keys: Making It Safe to Retry a Request
slides.body: Your payment request times out. Did it go through? You don't know — and if you retry blindly, you might charge the customer twice.

slides.title: A Timeout Is Genuinely Ambiguous
slides.body: The dangerous part of a network timeout isn't that it failed — it's that you don't know if it failed.
bullets: A request can time out because it never reached the server, or because it reached the server, was fully processed, and only the response got lost on the way back
For a read (GET a user's profile), retrying blindly is harmless — reading twice changes nothing

For a write with a real side effect (charge a card, place an order, send a payout), retrying blindly on the second case double-executes it — the client has no way to distinguish the two cases from its own vantage point

slides.title: Attach a Key, Let the Server Deduplicate
slides.body: The client generates a unique key per logical attempt (typically a UUID) and sends it with the request, usually as an `Idempotency-Key` header.
bullets: First time the server sees that key: it processes the request normally, executes the side effect, and stores the result keyed by that ID
Any retry that arrives with the same key: the server skips re-executing the side effect entirely and just returns the stored result from the first attempt

This shifts the guarantee from 'the network delivers the request exactly once' (impossible to guarantee) to 'the side effect executes exactly once, no matter how many times the request is retried' — which is achievable

slides.title: Naive Retry vs. Idempotency-Key Retry
slides.body: Same timeout, same retry — different outcome:

rows: Retry returns the original stored result

slides.title: Worked Example: A Payment API
slides.body: A checkout flow calls `POST /charges` with `Idempotency-Key: 8f14e...` and the charge times out client-side after 30 seconds.
bullets: The client's retry logic fires automatically, resending the exact same request with the exact same idempotency key
Server-side, the original charge had actually completed just after the client gave up waiting — the payment processor already moved the money

Because the retry carries the same key, the server recognizes it, skips creating a second charge, and returns the original charge's result — the customer is billed once, and the client still gets a clean success response

slides.title: What It Doesn't Solve
slides.body: Idempotency keys are a real safety mechanism, not a cure-all — a few sharp edges matter in practice.
bullets: Stored results can't live forever — servers set a TTL (often 24 hours) on idempotency records, so a retry arriving after that window is treated as a brand-new request

A server should validate that a retried request's body actually matches the original request for that key — otherwise a client bug that reuses a key with a different payload can silently return the wrong stored result instead of erroring

It only guarantees the operation itself executes once — it does not make a multi-step workflow (charge card, then reserve inventory, then send confirmation) atomic across all steps; that needs a separate pattern like sagas or the outbox pattern
The key has to be generated client-side per logical attempt, not per HTTP call — regenerating a fresh key on every retry defeats the entire purpose

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: A network timeout can't tell you whether your request succeeded server-side — that ambiguity is exactly what makes blind retries dangerous for anything with a side effect
Idempotency keys turn 'retry blindly' into a safe default: the client sends a stable key, the server stores and returns the first result on any repeat
This guarantees the side effect runs exactly once, regardless of how many times the network forces a retry
It doesn't make multi-step operations atomic, doesn't last forever (TTL-bound), and only works if the client reuses the same key across retries of the same logical attempt

questions.prompt: Why is a network timeout dangerous for a write request with a real side effect, but harmless for a read?
options: Timeouts never happen on reads
Reads change nothing on repeat, but a write's timeout leaves it ambiguous whether the side effect already happened before retrying
Writes are always slower than reads
There is no actual difference
questions.explanation: Retrying a read is always safe since reading twice changes nothing. Retrying a write blindly is risky because the original request may have already succeeded server-side, and a retry could execute the side effect a second time.

questions.prompt: What does the server do when it receives a second request carrying an idempotency key it has already seen?
options: It re-executes the side effect a second time
It rejects the request with an error
It skips re-executing the side effect and returns the stored result from the first time it saw that key
It ignores the key entirely
questions.explanation: The core mechanism: the server stores the result keyed by the idempotency key on first receipt, and any retry with the same key gets that stored result instead of triggering the side effect again.

questions.prompt: What do idempotency keys NOT guarantee on their own?
options: That a single operation executes at most once
That a multi-step workflow spanning several separate operations is atomic end-to-end
That retries are safe for that one operation
That a stored result can be returned on retry
questions.explanation: Idempotency keys make one operation safe to retry, but they don't coordinate multiple separate operations into one atomic unit — that requires a separate pattern like sagas or the outbox pattern.

posts.title: Circuit Breaker: Stopping One Slow Dependency From Taking Down Everything
posts.subtitle: When a downstream service gets slow instead of down, retries and thread pools quietly turn that into an outage for every service upstream — a circuit breaker cuts the connection before that happens.
posts.summary: A circuit breaker wraps a call to a dependency and tracks its recent failure rate. Once failures cross a threshold it 'opens' — failing fast locally instead of waiting on a dependency that's already struggling — then periodically lets a trial request through to check if the dependency recovered. The mechanism exists because slow failures, not hard-down ones, are what actually cascade: a hanging call ties up a thread or connection, and enough of those exhaust the caller's own capacity.

slides.title: Circuit Breaker: Stopping One Slow Dependency From Taking Down Everything
slides.body: A dependency that returns errors instantly is easy to handle. A dependency that just gets slow is what actually causes outages — because every caller keeps waiting.

slides.title: Cascading Failure Starts With a Slowdown, Not a Crash
slides.body: The dangerous failure mode in a service graph isn't a dependency returning 500s — it's one that stops responding at all.
bullets: Every in-flight call to the slow dependency holds a thread, a connection-pool slot, or a queue entry until it times out
If timeouts are long (or missing) and traffic keeps arriving, the caller's own thread pool or connection pool fills up entirely
Once that pool is exhausted, the caller can't serve requests for *any* dependency, including healthy ones — the failure has now spread one hop upstream
Repeat that at each layer and a single slow database or downstream API can stall an entire request graph

slides.title: Three States: Closed, Open, Half-Open
slides.body: A circuit breaker sits in front of a risky call and tracks outcomes, moving between three states.
bullets: Closed (normal): calls pass through; the breaker counts failures in a rolling window
Open (tripped): once failures cross a threshold, the breaker stops calling the dependency entirely and fails fast — callers get an immediate error or fallback instead of waiting on a timeout
Half-Open (probing): after a cooldown period, the breaker lets a small number of trial requests through; if they succeed it closes again, if they fail it reopens and waits longer

slides.title: A Payment Service Under Load, With Real Numbers
slides.body: Netflix's Hystrix library popularized concrete, tunable defaults for exactly this pattern.
bullets: Rolling window: track the last 10 seconds of calls, requiring at least 20 requests in that window before the breaker can trip (too few samples shouldn't trigger a decision)
Error threshold: if 50% or more of those calls fail or time out, the breaker opens
Sleep window: once open, wait 5 seconds before allowing a single half-open probe request through

Effect: instead of every request queuing behind a struggling payment API for its full 30-second timeout, requests fail in milliseconds and the caller can show a fallback ('payment queued, we'll confirm shortly') instead of hanging

slides.title: Circuit Breaker vs Retry vs Timeout vs Bulkhead
slides.body: These patterns are complementary, not competing — most production systems use all four together.

rows: Bounds how long one call can hang
Doesn't stop you from repeatedly hitting a dependency that's already failing
Re-attempts a failed call, sometimes with backoff
Can amplify load on an already-struggling dependency if used without a breaker
Stops calling a dependency once it's clearly unhealthy, failing fast instead
Doesn't fix the dependency — only limits the blast radius while it recovers
Isolates resources (thread pools, connections) per dependency
Doesn't detect failure — just contains it once the breaker or timeout reveals it

slides.title: Where Circuit Breakers Go Wrong
slides.body: The pattern is simple; tuning it for a real system is the hard part.
bullets: Thresholds set too sensitive cause 'flapping' — the breaker opens and closes repeatedly on normal traffic noise instead of real degradation
One breaker shared across multiple unrelated calls means an unrelated dependency's failure trips the breaker for calls that were fine
A breaker with no fallback just turns a slow error into a fast one — real resilience needs a meaningful fallback (cached data, a queued retry, a degraded response), not just failing faster
Skipping it for internal calls because 'it's just our own service' — internal dependencies cascade exactly the same way external ones do

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: The failure that cascades is usually a slow dependency holding resources open, not a dependency that fails instantly
A circuit breaker has three states — closed, open, half-open — and moves between them based on a rolling failure-rate window, not a single failed call
Use one breaker per dependency, not one global breaker, so unrelated failures don't cross-contaminate
A breaker without a real fallback only makes failures faster, not less disruptive — pair it with a fallback, and with retries/timeouts/bulkheads, not instead of them

questions.prompt: Why is a slow, hanging dependency more dangerous to a system than one that fails instantly?
options: Slow calls use more CPU than fast failures
Slow calls hold threads, connections, or queue slots open until they time out, which can exhaust the caller's own capacity and spread the failure upstream
Slow calls are always caused by network issues
Instant failures always crash the calling service
questions.explanation: An instant failure frees up the caller's resources right away. A hanging call ties up a thread or connection slot for its full timeout, and if enough calls pile up, the caller's own resource pool is exhausted — turning one slow dependency into an outage for every caller upstream.

questions.prompt: In the classic three-state circuit breaker model, what happens in the Half-Open state?
options: All traffic is blocked permanently
All traffic flows normally with no monitoring
A limited number of trial requests are allowed through to check if the dependency has recovered, deciding whether to close or reopen the breaker
The breaker doubles its failure threshold
questions.explanation: Half-Open is a probing state: after the cooldown (sleep window) following an Open state, the breaker lets a small number of test requests through. Success moves it back to Closed; continued failure sends it back to Open with a fresh cooldown.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't adding retries alone protect a system from cascading failure?
options: Retries are only useful for read requests
Retries without a circuit breaker can pile more load onto a dependency that's already struggling, making the overload worse
Retries always succeed on the second attempt
Retries are deprecated in modern distributed systems
questions.explanation: A retry re-sends a failed request, which is fine if the failure was transient — but if the dependency is genuinely overloaded, blind retries from every caller multiply the load on it. A circuit breaker stops the retries once it's clear the dependency isn't recovering.

posts.title: MCP Authorization: Trust Without a Shared Secret
posts.subtitle: A remote MCP server can't inherit your OS login the way a local one does — OAuth 2.1 fills that gap, and getting it wrong opens a confused-deputy hole.
posts.summary: A local MCP server over stdio inherits the trust of whoever launched the process — there's no network hop to secure. A remote MCP server over HTTP has no such luxury, so the spec layers OAuth 2.1 on top: dynamic client registration, PKCE, and — critically — Resource Indicators (RFC 8707) that bind a token to one specific server so a compromised or malicious server can't replay it elsewhere. Skipping that last piece is what turns a normal OAuth flow into a confused-deputy vulnerability.

slides.title: MCP Authorization: Trust Without a Shared Secret
slides.body: A local tool server trusts you because it's running as you. A remote one over the network has no such guarantee — it has to be told, cryptographically, who's allowed to call it.

slides.title: stdio Had It Easy — HTTP Doesn't
slides.body: Most early MCP servers ran as a local subprocess talking over stdio. That transport gets authorization for free.
bullets: A stdio server is spawned by the client on the user's own machine — the OS process boundary and the user's login are the entire trust model, no tokens needed
A remote HTTP/SSE server is reachable by anyone who can route to its URL — without an explicit check, any client could call tools bound to another user's calendar, repo, or database
MCP's authorization spec exists specifically to close that gap for the remote/HTTP case, not for local stdio servers

slides.title: The Flow: OAuth 2.1, With the Server as the Resource
slides.body: A remote MCP server is treated as an OAuth 2.1 protected resource, and the client that wants to call it is an OAuth client — the same roles as a normal 'login with X' flow, aimed at a tool endpoint instead of a UI.
bullets: The client fetches the server's metadata to discover which authorization server issues tokens for it
It dynamically registers itself with that authorization server (RFC 7591) instead of needing a pre-shared client ID
It runs an authorization-code flow with PKCE — no client secret required, safe for public/native clients like a desktop agent
The resulting access token is scoped to the MCP server's own resource identifier, not left open-ended

slides.title: The Confused Deputy: Why the Token's Audience Matters
slides.body: The subtle failure mode isn't a missing token — it's a token that works somewhere it shouldn't.
bullets: Token passthrough: an MCP server accepts a token that was actually issued for a different API, then forwards it upstream — the upstream API trusts it because the token is genuinely valid, just not meant for this caller
Resource Indicators (RFC 8707) fix this by having the client request a token whose 'audience' is bound to the specific MCP server's URL, and having the server reject any token not addressed to it
Without that binding, a malicious or compromised MCP server becomes a 'confused deputy' — it has a legitimate credential and no way to tell it was handed one meant for someone else

slides.title: Local vs Remote: Different Transports, Different Trust Models

rows: None — the client spawned the server itself
Network — any client that can reach the URL

slides.title: Connecting an Agent to a Remote Calendar Server
slides.body: A concrete walk-through for a desktop AI agent adding a remote MCP calendar server.
bullets: 1. Agent adds the server URL; the server returns 401 with a pointer to its authorization server's metadata
2. Agent dynamically registers as a client, then opens a browser for the user to log in and approve access
3. Agent completes the PKCE code exchange and receives an access token whose audience is that one calendar server's resource URL
4. Every tool call carries that token; the server verifies both signature and audience before running create_event or list_events
5. If the agent later adds a second, unrelated MCP server, it must repeat the flow — the calendar token is refused there by design

slides.title: Where Implementations Go Wrong
slides.body: The spec is precise about this because the failure mode is easy to build by accident.
bullets: Skipping audience validation: a server that checks 'is this token signed by an authorization server I trust?' but not 'was this token issued for me?' is exploitable via token passthrough
Reusing one long-lived token across every MCP server an agent talks to, instead of a distinct, narrowly-scoped token per server
Treating stdio's implicit trust as a reason to skip auth on a server that's later exposed over HTTP for remote access — the transport change silently removes the safety net
Storing tokens without expiry or revocation, so a leaked token stays valid indefinitely

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: stdio MCP servers get authorization for free from the OS process boundary; HTTP/SSE servers need it explicitly because they're network-reachable
MCP's authorization model is standard OAuth 2.1 + PKCE + dynamic client registration — nothing MCP-specific, which is the point: reuse a well-audited protocol
Resource Indicators (RFC 8707) binding a token's audience to one specific server is what prevents the confused-deputy / token-passthrough failure
When reviewing an MCP server implementation, the first question to ask is: does it check *who the token was issued for*, not just whether it's validly signed

questions.prompt: Why don't local stdio MCP servers need an OAuth flow?
options: Because stdio is encrypted by default
Because the client spawns the server as a local subprocess, so the OS process boundary and user session are the trust model — there's no network hop to secure
Because stdio servers can't access sensitive data
Because OAuth only works over HTTPS
questions.explanation: A stdio server runs as a subprocess of the client, inheriting the launching user's OS-level trust. There's no separate network identity to authenticate — that requirement only appears once a server is reachable remotely over HTTP/SSE.

questions.prompt: What specifically does a 'token passthrough' / confused-deputy attack exploit?
options: A weak password on the authorization server
An expired token that the server fails to reject
A validly-signed token whose audience isn't checked, so it works on a server it wasn't issued for
A missing TLS certificate on the MCP server
questions.explanation: The token is genuinely valid and properly signed — the bug is that the receiving server never checks whether the token's audience (Resource Indicator) actually names it, so a token meant for one resource gets accepted, and potentially forwarded, by another.

questions.prompt: What role does PKCE play in the MCP authorization flow?
options: It encrypts the MCP tool call payloads
It replaces the need for dynamic client registration
It lets a public client (like a desktop agent with no way to keep a secret safe) complete an OAuth code exchange securely without a client secret
It sets the token's expiry time
questions.explanation: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) binds the authorization request to the eventual token exchange with a locally-generated verifier, so a public client — one that can't safely hold a static client secret, like a desktop or mobile agent — can still prove it's the same party that started the flow.

posts.title: Quantization: Running a 70B Model on One GPU
posts.subtitle: Cutting weights from 16-bit floats to 4-bit integers shrinks memory 4x — if you handle the outliers correctly.
posts.summary: Quantization compresses an LLM's weights from 16-bit floats down to 8-bit or 4-bit integers, cutting memory and memory-bandwidth use by 2-4x with little accuracy loss when done carefully. The hard part is a small set of extreme-magnitude 'outlier' activations that naive rounding destroys — methods like LLM.int8(), GPTQ, and AWQ each handle that outlier problem differently, trading calibration cost against quality.

slides.title: Quantization: Running a 70B Model on One GPU
slides.body: Storing every weight as a 16-bit float is wasteful. Round them into fewer bits and a model that needed four GPUs fits on one — if you're careful about which weights you round.

slides.title: Memory, Not Compute, Is the Bottleneck
slides.body: LLM inference is usually memory-bandwidth bound: the GPU spends more time moving weights from memory than multiplying them. Smaller weights mean less to move.
bullets: fp16 stores each weight in 2 bytes — a 70B-parameter model needs roughly 140GB just for weights, before KV cache or activations
A single H100/A100 has 80GB of memory — you need at least two just to load the weights
Quantizing to INT8 halves that to ~70GB; INT4 quarters it to ~35GB, small enough for one GPU with headroom for the KV cache

slides.title: Weight-Only Quantization: Compress Storage, Dequantize on the Fly
slides.body: The dominant approach for inference doesn't touch training. It rounds stored weights to fewer bits, then converts back to fp16 right before each matrix multiply.
bullets: Post-training quantization (PTQ): no retraining — calibrate on a few hundred sample sequences, then round. Takes GPU-minutes to hours
Quantization-aware training (QAT): simulates quantization during a full retraining run — better quality floor, far more expensive
PTQ is the default for deploying an already-trained model; QAT is reserved for cases where PTQ quality isn't good enough

slides.title: The Outlier Problem: Why Naive Rounding Breaks Big Models
slides.body: Past a few billion parameters, LLM activations develop a small number of feature dimensions with far larger magnitude than the rest, concentrated in specific channels.
bullets: A shared quantization range has to stretch to cover those outliers, which crushes the resolution available for every normal-magnitude weight
The result: a handful of channels wreck accuracy for the whole layer if you quantize everything uniformly
LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al.) fixes this with mixed-precision decomposition — outlier channels stay in fp16, everything else quantizes to int8

slides.title: GPTQ vs AWQ: Two Ways to Protect What Matters
slides.body: Both are one-shot PTQ methods that push weights to 4-bit, but they identify and protect 'important' weights differently.

rows: Rounds each weight independently, no correction
Fastest, but noticeable quality loss in outlier-heavy layers
Quantizes layer-by-layer; after each weight is rounded, adjusts the remaining unquantized weights using second-order (Hessian) error info
Strong quality; calibration is slower — walks weights one at a time
Finds the ~1% of weight channels most correlated with large activations and scales them up before rounding, protecting them from precision loss
Faster calibration than GPTQ, comparable quality, widely used for on-device deployment

slides.title: Fitting a 7B Chat Model on a 24GB Consumer GPU
slides.body: A concrete sizing example for a single RTX 4090 or similar 24GB card.
bullets: fp16: 7B params x 2 bytes ≈ 14GB for weights alone — leaves under 10GB for KV cache, so long conversations or larger batches won't fit
INT4 (GPTQ or AWQ): the same weights shrink to ≈3.5GB
That frees up over 20GB for KV cache and activations — enough headroom for much longer context windows or serving several requests at once on the same card

slides.title: When Quantization Bites Back
slides.body: Quantization is not a free lunch — the failure modes are subtle and easy to miss if you only check perplexity.
bullets: Accuracy loss isn't uniform: multi-step reasoning and math degrade faster than fluency and chit-chat at the same bit-width
Below INT4 (INT3, INT2) quality drops sharply for most models without specialized techniques
Calibration data matters — calibrating on generic web text and then deploying on code or another language can quietly hurt exactly the traffic you care about
Many kernels still dequantize back to fp16 before the actual matmul, so you save memory and bandwidth, but not full compute (FLOPs) — real compute speedups need INT4-native kernels

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Quantization mainly buys memory and memory-bandwidth — the actual bottleneck for most LLM inference, not raw compute
INT8 is close to lossless; INT4 (GPTQ or AWQ) is the practical sweet spot for most deployments; below that needs specialized care
The outlier problem — a few extreme-magnitude activation channels — is why naive rounding fails on large models, and why GPTQ/AWQ/LLM.int8() exist
Always evaluate quantized models on your actual downstream tasks, not just perplexity — perplexity can look fine while task accuracy quietly drops

questions.prompt: Why does a 70B-parameter model need roughly 140GB of memory in fp16?
options: Because each parameter is stored as a 2-byte (16-bit) float, so 70B x 2 bytes ≈ 140GB
Because the model actually has 140 billion parameters after tokenizer overhead
Because the KV cache doubles the raw parameter count
Because fp16 requires 4 bytes per parameter for memory alignment
questions.explanation: Each fp16 weight takes 2 bytes, so parameter count x 2 bytes gives the weight footprint: 70B x 2 bytes ≈ 140GB. That's before any KV cache or activation memory is added.

questions.prompt: What problem does LLM.int8()'s mixed-precision decomposition solve?
options: Slow tokenization caused by large vocabulary sizes
Catastrophic accuracy loss from a small number of extreme-magnitude activation outliers dominating a shared quantization range
KV cache eviction for very long contexts
Gradient explosion during quantization-aware training
questions.explanation: Large models develop a handful of outlier activation channels with far larger magnitude than the rest. Quantizing everything to one shared range wastes precision on those outliers and crushes resolution elsewhere — LLM.int8() keeps outlier channels in fp16 and quantizes the rest to int8.

questions.prompt: What's the main practical tradeoff between GPTQ and AWQ?
options: GPTQ requires full retraining while AWQ needs no calibration data at all
GPTQ corrects weights layer-by-layer using second-order (Hessian) information and is slower to calibrate; AWQ scales the weight channels most correlated with large activations and calibrates faster
AWQ only works on vision models while GPTQ only works on text models
GPTQ produces smaller files than AWQ at the same bit-width because it uses a different number format
questions.explanation: GPTQ walks through weights layer-by-layer, using second-order error information to correct what's left after each weight is quantized — powerful but slower to calibrate. AWQ instead identifies and protects the small set of weight channels most tied to large activations, trading some of that precision-correction for much faster calibration.

posts.title: J-Space: Anthropic Finds a Global Workspace in Claude
posts.subtitle: A Jacobian lens surfaces the small set of directions a model is 'poised to verbalize' — and ablating them collapses multi-step reasoning.
posts.summary: Anthropic's 'Verbalizable Representations Form a Global Workspace in Language Models' identifies J-space — a small, causally load-bearing subspace of a model's activations that holds whatever it can currently report, hold in mind, or reason with. Ablating it barely touches routine tasks like classification but collapses multi-hop reasoning, translation, and cipher-decoding below an unablated Haiku 4.5.

slides.title: There's a Workspace Hiding Inside Claude
slides.body: Anthropic built a tool that finds the handful of internal directions a model is actually 'thinking with' — as opposed to the much larger ocean of activity it can't report on or control.

slides.title: Most Interpretability Tools Show Correlation, Not Function
slides.body: Sparse autoencoders and probes can find directions that correlate with a concept, but they don't prove the model actually uses that direction to reason or act.
bullets: A model has billions of activation directions — most are 'automatic' processing the model can't verbalize or steer
Need: which directions are the model's actual working memory — held, reportable, and causally used downstream
Anthropic's answer: ask which directions causally raise the probability of a specific output word later, not just which correlate with it

slides.title: The Jacobian Lens: Read Directions by Their Causal Effect on Output
slides.body: For every word in the vocabulary, the J-lens computes which internal activation pattern makes the model more likely to say that word later — a Jacobian between hidden state and future output logits, not a static probe.
bullets: Surfaces 'verbalizable' directions: things the model could report, deliberately hold, or pass to downstream computation
The active set at any moment — J-space — holds only 10 to 25 concepts at once
That's under 10% of total activation variance carrying the reasoning load

slides.title: Three Zones, One Pass Through the Network
slides.body: Applying the J-lens across layers reveals a consistent geography, echoing the 'broadcast' structure of Global Workspace Theory from consciousness neuroscience.
bullets: Early layers: a 'sensory' zone parsing raw input tokens
Middle layers: the 'workspace' band — J-space, where abstract concepts persist and get manipulated
Final layers: a 'motor' zone where workspace contents collapse into the next output token

slides.title: Ablating J-Space: Some Tasks Shrug, Others Collapse
slides.body: Tasks that don't need held, manipulable intermediate state survive heavy ablation almost untouched. Tasks that require carrying state across steps fall apart.

rows: MMLU multiple choice, sentiment, extractive QA
Multi-hop reasoning, Caesar-cipher decoding, translation, summarization
Far more robust — steps are externalized into tokens

slides.title: Worked Example: Why Chain-of-Thought Text Is a Memory Prosthetic
slides.body: Ask Claude to Caesar-cipher-decode a sentence by shift 7, answering directly. It has to hold the running plaintext and shift count inside J-space — ablate J-space and the answer collapses.
bullets: Same task, but told to write out each decoded letter step by step: performance survives heavy ablation
Writing the intermediate state into tokens moves it out of the ~25-concept internal workspace and into the context window, which has no such capacity limit
Reframe: 'showing your work' isn't just for the reader — it's functionally expanding the model's own working memory

slides.title: Caveats: This Isn't Proof of Consciousness
slides.body: The paper checks functional signatures of Global Workspace Theory — report, deliberate holding, silent reasoning, generalization, selectivity — not subjective experience.
bullets: Independent replication is mixed: DeepMind's Neel Nanda published a more skeptical take on how strong the causal claims are
Demonstrated via open-sourced code and a Neuronpedia demo, but only on open-weight models — not full-scale claims on every model
Practical safety use (e.g. spotting concealed intent like 'fraud' or 'manipulation' in J-space even when output text looks cooperative) is early-stage, not a shipped product

slides.title: Why This Matters Beyond the Lab
bullets: Working memory in LLMs looks bounded — roughly a few dozen concepts — much like human working memory limits
Chain-of-thought isn't just an explanation format; ablation results suggest it functionally offloads reasoning state past that internal limit
A causal (not just correlational) interpretability lens opens a path to detecting concealed model intent, not just describing correlated features
Expect follow-up work probing whether J-space capacity predicts reasoning failures before they happen

questions.prompt: What does the Jacobian lens (J-lens) actually measure?
options: Attention weights between input tokens
Which internal activation directions causally raise the probability of a specific future output word
The size of the KV cache during generation
Gradient of the training loss with respect to model weights
questions.explanation: The J-lens is a Jacobian between a hidden state and future output-token logits — it identifies directions the model causally uses to produce specific words later, not just directions that correlate with a concept.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many concepts can J-space hold active at once?
options: 2 to 3
About 500
Unlimited — it scales with context length
questions.explanation: The paper reports J-space typically holds 10-25 active concepts, under 10% of total activation variance — a small, bounded working-memory-like capacity.

questions.prompt: Why does explicit chain-of-thought make cipher-decoding robust to J-space ablation, while answering directly doesn't?
options: Chain-of-thought uses a completely different part of the network that isn't ablated
Writing out each step externalizes intermediate state into context tokens instead of relying on the limited internal workspace
Chain-of-thought prompts automatically disable the ablation
Direct answers require more tokens, which increases ablation risk
questions.explanation: Ablating J-space removes the model's ability to hold intermediate state internally. Explicit CoT sidesteps this by writing that state into the context window, which isn't capacity-limited the way J-space is.

posts.title: Shieldstral: A Safety Classifier You Prompt, Not Retrain
posts.subtitle: Mistral's 3B open-weight moderation model takes your policy as a plain-language question at inference time — no fine-tuning per deployment.
posts.summary: Mistral released Shieldstral, a 3B-parameter open-weight multimodal safety classifier that reframes moderation as binary question-answering: you give it a plain-language policy question and it returns a calibrated yes/no safety score in one forward pass. It reportedly matches guard models up to 7x its size while running on a single 16GB GPU.

slides.title: A Safety Model That Reads Your Policy Instead of Baking It In
slides.body: Shieldstral, released August 4, 2026, ships as open weights under Apache 2.0 and turns moderation into a question you ask at inference time.

slides.title: Fixed Taxonomies Don't Travel Between Deployments
slides.body: Most guard models bake a fixed set of harm categories into their weights during training.
bullets: Re-targeting an existing guard model to a new policy usually means collecting data and retraining
Safety definitions differ by product, audience, and jurisdiction — there's no single 'correct' taxonomy to hard-code
Teams end up maintaining separate fine-tuned classifiers per use case, or over-broad ones that over-block

slides.title: Moderation as Binary Question-Answering
slides.body: At inference time you supply context, content, and a plain-language yes/no policy question — Shieldstral answers it.
bullets: Input: an evaluation context, a policy question in plain language, and the content — a prompt, a response, a prompt-response pair, or an image with optional text
The model emits logits for exactly two tokens, 'yes' and 'no'
Softmax-normalizing those two logits gives a continuous 0-1 safety score, thresholded at 0.5 for a verdict — one forward pass, one token, no generated explanation required

slides.title: What Ships
bullets: 3B parameters, multimodal (text and images)
Runs on a single 16GB GPU
Covers 12 languages
Open weights on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0

slides.title: Benchmark Claims

rows: Vs. guard models up to 7x larger

slides.title: Worked Example: Shipping a Custom Policy in an Afternoon
slides.body: A fintech app needs to catch responses that give specific investment advice without a disclaimer — a category no off-the-shelf guard model has a slot for.
bullets: With a fixed-taxonomy guard model: collect labeled examples, fine-tune, evaluate, redeploy
With Shieldstral: write the policy as a question — 'Does this response give specific personal investment advice without a disclaimer?' — and call the model
The same 3B weights now serve that policy alongside every other policy question the team writes, with zero additional training

slides.title: Tradeoffs to Know Before Deploying
bullets: A single yes/no token means no built-in explanation — auditing why something was flagged requires a separate call or process
Policy phrasing matters: an ambiguously worded question can shift the score, so policies need testing like prompts do
Benchmark numbers are Mistral's own reported figures, not yet independently replicated
Not a substitute for human review in legal, medical, or other high-stakes edge cases

slides.title: Why It Matters
bullets: Decouples 'what counts as unsafe' from the model weights — policy changes ship as text, not training runs
Small footprint (3B, 16GB GPU) makes on-device or per-request moderation viable at low latency
Signals a broader shift: guardrails as prompted classifiers rather than fixed-category models
Worth piloting anywhere you maintain more than one moderation policy across products or regions

questions.prompt: What core limitation of prior guard models does Shieldstral's design address?
options: They were too small to run on consumer hardware
They only supported English
Adapting them to a new safety policy usually required retraining because harm categories were fixed at training time
They could not process images
questions.explanation: Fixed-taxonomy guard models bake harm categories into their weights, so a new policy normally means new training data and a fine-tuning run. Shieldstral instead takes the policy as a plain-language question at inference time.

questions.prompt: How does Shieldstral produce its safety score?
options: It generates a full paragraph explaining its reasoning, then extracts a score
It runs the input through a separate classification head trained per category
It softmax-normalizes the logits of exactly two tokens, 'yes' and 'no', from a single forward pass
It averages scores from multiple sampled generations
questions.explanation: Shieldstral frames moderation as binary QA: it emits logits for 'yes' and 'no', softmax-normalizes them into a 0-1 score, and thresholds at 0.5 — one forward pass, one token, no generated explanation.

questions.prompt: What's a real tradeoff of the yes/no-token approach compared to a labeled-category output?
options: It cannot run on a single GPU
It doesn't provide a built-in explanation for why content was flagged, complicating audits
It only works on text, never images
It requires retraining for every new customer
questions.explanation: Because the verdict comes from just two token logits, there's no generated rationale by default — teams that need auditable explanations have to add a separate step.

posts.title: ReAct: Making an LLM Think Before Every Action
posts.subtitle: Interleaving Thought, Action, and Observation grounds an agent's reasoning in what actually happened — instead of what it assumed happened.
posts.summary: ReAct interleaves short reasoning steps with tool actions and real observations in a single loop, so an agent's plan gets checked against reality at every step instead of only at the end. On ALFWorld and WebShop it beat imitation- and RL-trained baselines by 34 and 10 absolute points in success rate, without any task-specific training.

slides.title: Reasoning Alone Drifts. Acting Alone Loops. ReAct Does Both.
slides.body: A simple prompting pattern — Thought, Action, Observation, repeat — that grounds an agent's reasoning in real feedback from its tools.

slides.title: Two Ways Agents Fail Without ReAct
bullets: Reasoning-only (pure chain-of-thought): the model reasons entirely from its own internal knowledge, ungrounded in the real world — small early errors compound into confident, wrong conclusions
Acting-only (tool calls with no explicit reasoning): the model fires off actions without planning or reflecting, so it repeats failed actions or loses track of the goal mid-task
Neither approach lets the model check a plan against fresh evidence before continuing

slides.title: The Loop: Thought, Action, Observation
slides.body: Each turn, the model writes a short thought (what to do next and why), takes one action from its tool set, and receives a real observation before thinking again.
bullets: Thought: 'I need the release date, so I should search for it'
Action: search('Shieldstral release date')
Observation: the real tool output gets appended to context — not a guess
The loop repeats until the model emits a Finish action with its answer

slides.title: Just a Prompting Pattern, No New Architecture
bullets: Works with any instruction-following base model — nothing about the weights changes
The full trajectory (every prior thought/action/observation) stays in context and is re-fed each step
Thoughts serve two jobs: inducing/updating the action plan, and handling exceptions when an action's result is unexpected
Actions are what connect the model to ground truth — a search API, a calculator, a code executor, a database query

slides.title: What the Original Paper Measured
slides.body: Yao et al. (2022) tested ReAct on knowledge tasks (HotpotQA, FEVER, with Wikipedia API access) and decision-making tasks (ALFWorld, WebShop).
bullets: On HotpotQA and FEVER: ReAct clearly beat act-only prompting and matched chain-of-thought's accuracy, while producing far more grounded, less hallucinated reasoning traces
On ALFWorld and WebShop: one- and two-shot ReAct prompting beat imitation- and reinforcement-learning baselines trained on roughly 100,000 task instances

slides.title: Worked Example: Answering a Multi-Hop Question
slides.body: "What is the elevation range of the area that the eastern sector of the Colorado orogeny extends into?"
bullets: Thought: I need to find what the eastern sector extends into, then its elevation range — search first
Action: search('Colorado orogeny eastern sector')
Observation: '...eastern sector extends into the High Plains...'
Thought: now I need the High Plains' elevation range
Action: search('High Plains elevation range') → Observation: '1,800 to 7,000 ft' → Finish('1,800 to 7,000 ft')

slides.title: When ReAct Struggles
bullets: Non-informative observations (e.g. a search that returns nothing useful) can send the model down a repeated retry loop
Every thought and observation adds tokens — long trajectories get expensive and can eventually crowd out earlier context
It's still only as good as the tools it's given: a bad search API caps how grounded the reasoning can be
Doesn't fix flawed few-shot examples — the paper notes prompt quality still meaningfully affects trajectory quality

slides.title: Why ReAct Became the Default Agent Loop
bullets: Grounding reasoning in real observations, every step, catches errors before they compound
No fine-tuning required — it's a prompting/orchestration pattern, so it works the day you adopt it
It's the loop underneath most modern tool-calling agent frameworks, even when they don't say 'ReAct' by name
Pairs well with explicit memory or reflection steps for tasks longer than a handful of hops

questions.prompt: What is the core weakness of pure chain-of-thought reasoning that ReAct addresses?
options: It's too slow for real-time use
It's ungrounded in the real world, so small errors in internal knowledge compound into confidently wrong answers
It cannot be used with few-shot prompting
It only works on math problems
questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought reasons entirely from the model's internal knowledge with no way to check itself against the world, so errors and hallucinations compound across steps.

questions.prompt: In the Thought-Action-Observation loop, what does the Observation come from?
options: The model's own guess about what the action probably returned
A real result returned by executing the action (e.g. actual search results)
A summary generated by a second, separate model
The original user prompt, repeated
questions.explanation: The observation is the real output of executing the chosen action against an actual tool or environment — that's what grounds the next thought in reality instead of assumption.

questions.prompt: On ALFWorld and WebShop, how did one/two-shot ReAct prompting compare to imitation- and RL-trained baselines?
options: It performed worse, since it had no task-specific training
It performed about the same
It beat those baselines by 34 and 10 absolute points in success rate respectively, despite the baselines being trained on ~100,000 task instances
It only worked on ALFWorld, not WebShop
questions.explanation: Despite using only one or two in-context examples and no task-specific training, ReAct prompting outperformed baselines trained on roughly 10^5 task instances by 34 points on ALFWorld and 10 points on WebShop.

posts.title: XR-1: A Robot Policy Pretrained on Handheld Video, Not Robot Arms
posts.subtitle: Xiaomi Robotics skips the teleoperation bottleneck with 100K+ hours of embodiment-free footage.
posts.summary: XR-1 pretrains a vision-language-action robot policy on over 100,000 hours of real-world manipulation footage captured with a handheld rig instead of a robot arm, then aligns it to real embodiments with a much smaller second stage. On simulation benchmarks and real household tasks it beats prior VLA baselines, including Physical Intelligence's π0.5, especially when fine-tuning data is scarce.

slides.title: A Robot Policy Trained Mostly on Handheld Video, Not Robot Arms
slides.body: Xiaomi Robotics' XR-1 pretrains a vision-language-action model on over 100,000 hours of real-world manipulation footage captured with a handheld rig — no robot required — then aligns it to actual robot embodiments with a much smaller second stage.
bullets: Real teleoperated robot-arm data is slow and expensive to collect at scale — that's the actual bottleneck on scaling robot foundation models, not compute or model size
XR-1 sidesteps it: Stage 1 pretrains on UMI-captured handheld manipulation trajectories that need no physical robot at all
Stage 2 aligns the pretrained model to real robot embodiments using just 10K+ hours of cross-embodiment data — a fraction of the pretraining volume

slides.title: Embodied Robot Data Doesn't Scale Like Internet Text
slides.body: Every hour of teleoperated robot-arm demonstration requires a physical robot, an operator, and real time — there's no equivalent of scraping the web for it.
bullets: VLA models inherit a pretrained vision-language backbone (here, Qwen3-VL) but still need embodied action data to learn to actually move a robot arm
Collecting that data by teleoperating a real robot caps how much any single lab can gather, no matter how much compute they have
Prior scaling recipes for VLA models plateaued on data volume long before they plateaued on model or compute size

slides.title: Two-Stage Training: Cheap Video First, Real Robots Second
slides.body: XR-1 pairs a pretrained VLM with a Diffusion-Transformer action head through a Mixture-of-Transformers design, then trains it in two stages with very different data costs.
bullets: Stage 1 (pretraining): over 100,000 hours of real-world manipulation trajectories captured via UMI, a handheld/wearable rig — no robot embodiment needed to collect it
A VLM-powered auto-labeling pipeline segments these trajectories and writes natural-language descriptions of each scene-state transition, replacing manual annotation at this scale
Stage 2 (post-training): 10K+ hours of cross-embodiment robot data aligns the pretrained policy across specific robot embodiments and instructions
Architecture: a Qwen3-VL vision-language backbone plus a Diffusion-Transformer action head, joined via a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) design

slides.title: XR-1 vs. the Field on Simulation Benchmarks
slides.body: XR-1 ranks #1 on the public RoboCasa365 and RoboDojo leaderboards as of mid-July 2026, per the authors' own released results.

slides.title: Real-World Test: Four Household Tasks vs. π0.5
slides.body: The authors fine-tuned XR-1 and Physical Intelligence's π0.5 baseline on the same real household tasks, varying how much task-specific data each got.
bullets: With under 10 hours of task data: XR-1 hit 75% overall success across phone packing, printer refilling, laundry loading, and box packing — π0.5 hit 40%
Laundry loading specifically: XR-1 went from 80% to 100% success as fine-tuning data grew from under 10h to under 40h, while π0.5 only reached 50% at the higher budget
Box packing was the one task where π0.5 fully caught up — both models hit 100% at the under-40h budget, showing the pretraining edge narrows as embodiment-specific data grows

slides.title: What Embodiment-Free Pretraining Doesn't Solve
slides.body: Handheld capture removes the robot-arm bottleneck, but it doesn't remove every gap between video and deployment.
bullets: A handheld rig's grip and viewpoint differ physically from a robot gripper — Stage 2's cross-embodiment alignment is doing real work, not just fine-tuning, and still needs real robot data
The real-world comparison covered only 4 household manipulation tasks against one baseline (π0.5) — strong results here don't guarantee the same edge on tool use or long-horizon multi-step tasks
Auto-generated language labels from a VLM inherit that VLM's own blind spots and biases into every downstream policy trained on them

slides.title: The Bottleneck on Robot Learning Was Data Collection, Not Data Volume
bullets: The core insight: most of what a manipulation policy needs to learn — object interactions, scene dynamics — doesn't require a robot to observe, only a camera
Splitting training into cheap embodiment-free pretraining plus a small embodiment-specific alignment stage is a pattern likely to spread beyond this one paper
For real deployments, the practical payoff is data efficiency: XR-1 hit higher success rates than π0.5 using the same or less task-specific fine-tuning data

options: To pretrain the vision-language backbone from scratch
To align the pretrained policy across specific robot embodiments and instructions using cross-embodiment data
To generate the natural-language labels for Stage 1 data
To compress the model for faster inference

posts.title: Test-Time Compute: Trading Tokens for Accuracy at Inference
posts.subtitle: Why reasoning models let a fixed-size network think longer instead of just training it bigger.
posts.summary: Test-time compute scaling spends extra computation per query at inference — longer reasoning, more parallel samples, or explicit search — instead of only scaling the model's parameters and training data. It's the mechanism behind 'reasoning' models like o1-style and DeepSeek-R1-style systems, and it trades latency and cost for accuracy on hard problems, with sharp diminishing returns once the model's easy answer is already the popular one.

slides.title: A Fixed Model Can Get Smarter Without Retraining — If You Let It Think Longer
slides.body: Test-time compute scaling spends extra computation per query instead of per parameter: the same trained model answers hard problems by generating more reasoning, sampling more candidates, or searching more branches before committing to an answer.
bullets: Classic scaling law: bigger model + more training FLOPs = better average performance, same fixed cost at inference
Test-time scaling: same weights, but the cost now varies per query — easy questions get a fast answer, hard ones get thousands of extra 'thinking' tokens
This is the mechanism behind 'reasoning' models (o1-style, DeepSeek-R1-style, Gemini Thinking-style): they're trained specifically to make good use of a longer inference budget

slides.title: One-Shot Decoding Spends the Same Effort on Easy and Hard Problems
slides.body: A standard LLM emits its answer autoregressively in a single pass, with no built-in mechanism to notice 'this one is hard, I should try more approaches.'
bullets: Token budget for reasoning is fixed by training and prompt length, not by how hard the specific question actually is
A small arithmetic or logic slip early in a long derivation propagates uncorrected — there's no automatic retry or self-check
Labs historically scaled pretraining compute and parameter count to raise average accuracy; the compute spent per individual query at inference stayed nearly flat regardless of difficulty

slides.title: Three Families of Test-Time Compute
slides.body: All three trade extra inference compute for a better final answer, but they spend that compute in different shapes.
bullets: Sequential (longer chain-of-thought): the model generates far more intermediate reasoning tokens before answering, trained via RL to backtrack and double-check mid-generation — this is what dedicated 'thinking' models do
Parallel sampling (best-of-N / self-consistency): draw N independent full solutions at temperature > 0, then pick the majority answer or the one a verifier/reward model scores highest

Search (tree-of-thought / MCTS-style): branch at each reasoning step, score partial paths with a value function, and prune weak branches — closer to classic search algorithms than to plain autoregressive generation

slides.title: Worked Example: Solving a Hard Word Problem Three Ways
slides.body: Same model, same multi-step optimization word problem — three different test-time budgets, three different failure/success profiles.
bullets: One-shot: the model emits an answer directly; if it mis-sets up one equation, the wrong answer ships with full apparent confidence
Self-consistency (N=8): the model solves the problem 8 independent times at nonzero temperature; the numeric answer that shows up most often across those 8 runs is returned

Extended reasoning: the model writes a long scratchpad, notices its first equation double-counts a constraint, discards that branch, and re-derives — all inside one generation before producing the final answer

slides.title: Sequential vs. Parallel vs. Search

rows: Yes — a value/reward model to prune
Many short steps, harder to parallelize
Yes — RL on long reasoning traces
No — works on any base model
Usually yes — needs a trained verifier

slides.title: When Test-Time Compute Stops Paying Off
slides.body: More inference compute is not a free accuracy dial — it has sharp diminishing returns and real failure modes.
bullets: Diminishing returns: majority-vote gains flatten fast once N is large enough that the model's 'mode' answer is already the majority — extra samples beyond that just burn tokens and money
Latency-sensitive products (chat, autocomplete) often can't afford a generation that's 10x longer just to shave a few points off accuracy
Search and best-of-N are only as good as the verifier scoring candidates — a weak or miscalibrated verifier can confidently promote a wrong answer over a right one
Long reasoning traces can loop or ramble without ever converging, burning the entire token budget with no better final answer than a short generation would have given

slides.title: Compute Now Has Two Knobs, Not One
bullets: Training-time compute (bigger model, more data) raises the average; test-time compute (more thinking per query) raises the ceiling on individual hard problems

Pick sequential reasoning when you can afford one longer generation and want inline self-correction; pick parallel sampling when generations are cheap to run concurrently; reach for search only when you have a trustworthy verifier
The practical lesson for building on these models: budget tokens (and dollars) per query by difficulty, not as one flat setting for every request

questions.prompt: What's the core idea behind test-time compute scaling?
options: Training a bigger model on more data
Spending extra computation per query at inference instead of only at training time
Reducing the model's parameter count to save memory
Caching previous responses to skip recomputation
questions.explanation: Test-time compute scaling keeps the trained model fixed and instead lets it use more compute — longer reasoning, more samples, or search — for a specific query, trading inference cost for accuracy on that query.

questions.prompt: In self-consistency / best-of-N sampling, how is the final answer typically chosen?
options: The first completion the model generates
The completion with the fewest tokens
By majority vote across N independently sampled completions, or the one a verifier ranks highest
By averaging the raw logits of all N completions
questions.explanation: Self-consistency draws multiple independent reasoning paths at nonzero temperature and takes the most common final answer (or the one a reward/verifier model ranks highest) — diverse, non-repeating errors get outvoted by the correct answer showing up more consistently.

questions.prompt: Which test-time compute approach most depends on having a trained value/verifier model to work well?
options: Sequential chain-of-thought extension
Search-based methods like tree-of-thought / MCTS-style reasoning
Greedy one-shot decoding
Simple prompt truncation
questions.explanation: Search methods branch into multiple partial reasoning paths and need a value function or verifier to score and prune those branches — without a good verifier, the search can't tell a promising partial path from a dead end.

posts.title: MCP Sampling: A Server Borrows the Client's Model
posts.subtitle: The primitive that lets a tool server 'think' without ever holding its own API key.
posts.summary: Sampling is the MCP primitive that runs in the opposite direction from Tools: instead of a client asking a server to do something, a server asks the client to run an LLM completion on its behalf. The client — not the server — picks the actual model and can insert a human-approval step before anything runs. That means servers never need their own API key, and users keep control over which model sees their data and what it's allowed to generate.

slides.title: Most MCP Primitives Flow One Way — Sampling Flows Back
slides.body: Tools, Resources, and Prompts all exist for the client's LLM to reach into a server. Sampling is the mirror image: a server that needs an LLM to do some thinking asks the client to run one for it.
bullets: Declared as a client capability during MCP's initialize handshake — a server has to check for it before relying on it
The request travels server → client, the opposite direction of a normal tool call
It exists so servers can 'think' without shipping their own model, API key, or billing relationship

slides.title: A Tool Server Sometimes Needs an LLM It Doesn't Have
slides.body: Plenty of useful server-side logic isn't deterministic code — it's judgment: summarizing, classifying, drafting. Without sampling, a server has three bad options.
bullets: Ship its own API key and pay for every call itself — an ops burden and a cost the server author didn't sign up for
Force the user to configure a second, separate model just for this one server — friction that kills adoption
Punt the judgment call back to the client's main LLM as a giant tool result and hope it handles it well — wasteful and imprecise

slides.title: sampling/createMessage: Ask the Client to Run the Completion
slides.body: A server that needs a generation sends a sampling/createMessage request over the same JSON-RPC connection, and the client decides how to fulfill it.
bullets: Request carries messages (the conversation so far), an optional systemPrompt, maxTokens, and modelPreferences — hints plus 0-1 priorities for cost, speed, and intelligence, not a hard model name
The CLIENT resolves modelPreferences to an actual model — a server can ask for 'fast and cheap' or 'most capable' but never dictates the exact model
includeContext lets the server request none, thisServer's context, or allServers' context be attached — the client still governs what's actually shared

slides.title: The Round Trip Has a Human Checkpoint Built In
slides.body: Because a server is effectively spending the user's model budget and attention, the spec expects the client to keep a human in the loop.
bullets: 1. Server sends sampling/createMessage with the draft messages and preferences
2. Client MAY show the user the outgoing request for review/edit before it ever reaches a model
3. Client calls whichever LLM it resolved the preferences to (its own configured model, not the server's choice)
4. Client MAY show the user the completion before returning it, then sends the result back to the server

slides.title: A Meeting-Notes Server With No Model of Its Own
slides.body: An MCP server exposes a summarize_transcript tool that condenses a 40-minute call into five action items.
bullets: Instead of embedding an OpenAI key, the tool handler issues one sampling/createMessage call with the transcript and a systemPrompt asking for action items
The client resolves that to whatever model the user already pays for — their Claude subscription, say — so the server never touches billing or credentials
The user's client can surface the outgoing prompt first, so a transcript with sensitive names doesn't silently leave the device without a glance

slides.title: Sampling vs. a Server Holding Its Own API Key

rows: Whoever the client's model subscription belongs to
Resolved by the client from preferences/hints
Client can show the prompt and result before either fires
Server must store and protect a key
Server never holds a model credential at all

slides.title: Sampling Is Optional and Adds a Real Round Trip
slides.body: It's easy to design a server that assumes sampling is always there. The protocol doesn't promise that.
bullets: Support is an optional client capability — many hosts don't implement it, so a server depending on it needs a fallback (e.g. degrade the feature, or ask the user directly)
Every sampling call is a full round trip through the client, plus an optional human-approval pause — noticeably slower than a server calling a model directly
Results aren't deterministic across clients: the same server prompt can hit a different model depending on whose client is connected, so outputs will vary

Because the server crafts the messages, a compromised or careless server can still attempt prompt injection against the client's model — sampling moves who pays, not who's responsible for reviewing the prompt

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Sampling flows server → client: a server asks the client to run an LLM completion instead of calling a model itself
The client — not the server — resolves modelPreferences to an actual model, and can review both the outgoing prompt and the completion
Servers gain zero-key, zero-billing access to 'thinking' — at the cost of an optional capability, real latency, and no determinism guarantee
It doesn't remove the need for prompt-injection care — the server still authors what the client's model will see

questions.prompt: Which direction does an MCP sampling request travel?
options: Client to server, like a normal tool call
Server to client — the server asks the client to run a completion
Server to server, bypassing the client entirely
It's a broadcast to every connected MCP server at once
questions.explanation: Sampling is the mirror image of a tool call: the server sends sampling/createMessage to the client, asking the client to run an LLM completion on its behalf.

questions.prompt: A server sets modelPreferences with a high intelligencePriority. What actually decides which model runs?
options: The server, which names an exact model in the request
The preference value directly maps to a fixed model ID chosen by the MCP spec
The client, which resolves the hints and priorities to whichever model it has configured
Whichever model responds fastest to a race between multiple providers
questions.explanation: modelPreferences are hints and 0-1 priorities (cost, speed, intelligence), not a model name. The client is the one that resolves them to an actual model it has access to.

questions.prompt: Why can't a server assume every MCP client supports sampling?
options: Sampling was deprecated in favor of Tools
It's an optional client capability that must be checked for and isn't implemented by every host
Sampling only works with open-weight models
Servers must pay a licensing fee to use sampling
questions.explanation: Like Roots, sampling is declared as an optional capability during the initialize handshake. A server that depends on it needs a sensible fallback for clients that don't support it.

posts.title: InferenceBench: Grid Search Beats the AI Agent
posts.subtitle: Frontier agents shipped vLLM in 94% of runs — then stopped optimizing
posts.summary: InferenceBench gives an AI agent one H100 GPU, a target LLM, and a two-hour clock, then scores it on how much it can speed up real LLM inference across four latency/throughput scenarios. The surprising result: plain, non-agentic hyperparameter search (SMAC3, TPE) beat every frontier LLM agent tested, even though the agents reliably picked good tooling like vLLM.

slides.title: Can an Agent Actually Speed Up LLM Inference From Scratch?
slides.body: InferenceBench hands an autonomous coding agent one H100, a target model, and a two-hour clock, then asks it to act as an ML systems engineer: stand up the fastest possible OpenAI-compatible inference server.

slides.title: Most ‘Open-Ended’ Agent Benchmarks Aren't
slides.body: The authors' core complaint: many nominally open-ended engineering benchmarks can be solved by retrieving a well-known recipe and nudging a couple of hyperparameters, so a high score doesn't prove the agent optimized anything — it might just have memorized the answer.
bullets: InferenceBench is scored on hard, verifiable metrics (latency, throughput) instead of subjective task completion
Four separate scenarios each isolate one bottleneck, so there's no single ‘known recipe’ that wins everywhere
Built by Jehyeok Yeon, Ben Rank, and Maksym Andriushchenko; presented at ICML 2026's Agents in the Wild workshop

slides.title: Four Scenarios, One Fixed Budget
bullets: Every agent gets the same target LLM, one H100, and a hard two-hour wall-clock budget — no re-runs, no do-overs
Output must be a real, running OpenAI-compatible server that also passes quality and integrity gates, not just a config file

slides.title: A Non-Agent Search Beat Every Frontier Agent
slides.body: SMAC3 and TPE never write code or reason about the system — they just try configurations of vLLM's existing knobs. Both beat every LLM agent tested.

slides.title: Agents Found the Right Tool, Then Stopped
slides.body: 93.9% of agent runs independently chose to serve with vLLM — the same call a systems engineer would make. But having picked it, most agents left it close to default rather than pushing the knobs that separate a 6x run from an 11x one: KV-cache block size, batching limits, quantization choices, parallelism settings.
bullets: The gap isn't ‘agents don't know good tools’ — it's ‘agents under-explore once they've found one’
A blind grid/Bayesian search has no such instinct to stop early; it keeps sampling configurations until the clock runs out

slides.title: What This Result Doesn't Prove
bullets: It's a two-hour, single-GPU, single-task snapshot — not a claim that agents can never out-search a hyperparameter sweep
The task is unusually clean and verifiable (latency/throughput are easy to score); most real engineering work isn't
SMAC3/TPE are purpose-built optimizers with no reasoning overhead — a fairer test might pair an agent WITH a search tool rather than against one
Only a handful of frontier agents were tested; the ranking could shift as new agent harnesses ship

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: InferenceBench asks agents to optimize real LLM-serving latency/throughput under a strict time and hardware budget
Every tested frontier agent lost to plain hyperparameter search (SMAC3: 11.53x vs. Claude Sonnet 4.6's 8.08x)
Agents reliably picked good tooling (vLLM, 93.9% of runs) but didn't push exploration as far as a dedicated search algorithm
A useful reality check on ‘agents will automate ML engineering’ claims — reaching for the right library isn't the same as optimizing it

questions.prompt: What is InferenceBench actually asking an agent to do?
options: Answer multiple-choice ML trivia questions
Deploy and optimize a real OpenAI-compatible LLM inference server under a time and GPU budget
Fine-tune a model on a labeled dataset
Write unit tests for an existing inference server
questions.explanation: The agent must produce a genuinely running, OpenAI-compatible server and is scored on hard latency/throughput metrics — not a static config or a narrow prescribed workflow.

questions.prompt: According to the paper, what beat every frontier LLM agent on aggregate speedup?
options: A larger LLM agent (GPT-5)
Non-agent hyperparameter search methods (SMAC3, TPE)
Manual expert tuning by the paper's authors
Running the default vLLM configuration
questions.explanation: SMAC3 (11.53x) and TPE (11.25x) — both black-box hyperparameter search methods with no code reasoning — outperformed the best agent, Claude Sonnet 4.6, at 8.08x.

questions.prompt: What does the 93.9%-vLLM statistic actually show?
options: That agents can't use serving frameworks at all
That agents chose reasonable tools but often didn't push optimization far beyond defaults
That vLLM is required to pass the benchmark
That agents outperformed hyperparameter search
questions.explanation: Nearly every agent correctly reached for vLLM as the serving backend — good tool selection — but that alone left them behind the non-agent search methods, which kept tuning long after an agent would typically stop.

posts.title: Kimi K3: Moonshot Ships the Largest Open LLM
posts.subtitle: 2.8T parameters, 104B active, 1M context — and the full weights are free
posts.summary: Moonshot AI released full, downloadable weights for Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with a 1-million-token context window — the largest open-weight model publicly available. It's built on two new mechanisms, Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals, and Moonshot's own benchmarks put it near, but not at, the very top of the frontier.

slides.title: The Biggest Open-Weight LLM Ever Released
slides.body: Moonshot AI published full, downloadable weights for Kimi K3 — a 2.8-trillion-parameter model with a 1,048,576-token context window — making it the largest open-weight model publicly available.

slides.title: 104B Active, Not 2.8T — Here's Why That Matters
slides.body: K3 is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model: only 16 of its 896 experts fire for any given token, so a token's actual compute cost tracks the 104B active parameters, not the 2.8T stored on disk.
bullets: 93 total layers: 69 use Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), a linear-attention variant; 24 use Gated Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)
KDA keeps per-token attention cost from growing quadratically — what makes a 1M-token context window tractable at all
Attention Residuals (AttnRes) replace uniform residual connections with selective retrieval of relevant representations across depth
Native multimodal input: text, images, and video go through the same model, no separate vision adapter bolted on

slides.title: Where K3 Actually Scores
slides.body: These are Moonshot's own reported benchmark numbers.
bullets: Moonshot says K3 performs “competitively” with Anthropic's Fable 5 and outperforms Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.6 Sol/5.5 — but stops short of claiming the top spot outright

slides.title: What 16-of-896 Routing Looks Like for One Token
slides.body: Feed K3 a token inside a stack trace. The router scores all 896 experts, picks the 16 most relevant — say, ones specialized in code syntax, error patterns, and control flow — and only those 16 run their feed-forward pass, instead of all 896.
bullets: Same trick every production MoE model uses (Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, GLM) — K3's contribution is doing it at unprecedented total scale
Deployable today via vLLM, SGLang, or Moonshot's own CLI, with an OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible API for drop-in testing

slides.title: Free Weights, Not a Free Lunch
bullets: “Open-weight” here means the Kimi K3 License, a custom license — not Apache 2.0 or MIT, so check terms before commercial redistribution
2.8T parameters is still hundreds of GB of weights to store and load, even with only 104B active — this is not a laptop model
Moonshot's own benchmarks position K3 behind Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol on overall capability; it wins on being freely downloadable, not on topping every leaderboard
A brand-new attention mechanism (KDA) means less battle-tested tooling and fewer documented failure modes than standard attention

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Kimi K3: 2.8T total / 104B active MoE, 1M-token context, built on Kimi Delta Attention + Attention Residuals
Full weights are public on Hugging Face under the Kimi K3 License — self-hostable via vLLM/SGLang
Benchmarks (GPQA 93.5, MCPMark 94.5) put it near the frontier, though Moonshot itself says it still trails the very top closed models
The real story is scale-at-openness: nobody has released weights this large before

questions.prompt: How many of Kimi K3's 896 experts are active for a given token?
questions.explanation: Only 16 experts fire per token — that's what makes 104B ‘active’ parameters out of 2.8T total; the rest sit idle until routed to.

questions.prompt: What problem does Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) mainly solve?
options: Reducing the number of experts needed
Keeping attention cost from growing quadratically so a 1M-token context is feasible
Adding vision support to a text-only model
Replacing the need for a tokenizer
questions.explanation: KDA is a linear-attention variant. Standard attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, which would make a million-token context prohibitively expensive; KDA keeps that cost near-linear.

questions.prompt: What does ‘open-weight’ NOT guarantee about a model like Kimi K3?
options: That anyone can download the weights
That the architecture is documented
That the license permits unrestricted commercial use
That inference code exists for it
questions.explanation: K3 ships under a custom Kimi K3 License, not a permissive OSI license like Apache 2.0 — downloadable weights don't automatically mean unrestricted commercial rights.
