posts.title: GLM-5.2: Open-Weight Coding at a Sixth of GPT-5.5's Cost
posts.subtitle: 1M-token context and sparse attention, released under Apache-2.0
posts.summary: Zhipu AI (Z.ai) open-sourced GLM-5.2 under Apache-2.0: a 744B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model (40B active) with a stable 1M-token context enabled by a new sparse-attention scheme called IndexShare. On SWE-Bench Pro it scores 62.1 versus GPT-5.5's 58.6, at roughly a sixth of GPT-5.5's per-token API price.

slides.title: GLM-5.2: Zhipu AI's Open-Weight Coding Flagship
slides.body: Released by Z.ai (Zhipu AI) under Apache-2.0, GLM-5.2 pairs a 1M-token context with coding benchmark scores that beat a closed frontier model.
bullets: 744B total parameters, 40B active per token (Mixture-of-Experts)
1M-token context window via a new sparse-attention scheme
Outscores GPT-5.5 on SWE-Bench Pro at roughly a sixth of the per-token cost

slides.title: Long-Horizon Coding Agents Blow Up Cost and Context
slides.body: Agentic coding sessions can run for thousands of turns, with every turn re-sending the full transcript — that's brutal for both context limits and API bills.
bullets: Closed frontier pricing is steep: GPT-5.5 runs about $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens
Most open-weight models plateau around 128K-256K context — too short to hold a full repo plus a long agent trace
Dense attention makes a 1M-token context extremely expensive to serve, which is why so few models offer one

slides.title: IndexShare: One Indexer Shared Across Every 4 Layers
slides.body: GLM-5.2 builds on DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), adding IndexShare — reusing a single sparse-attention indexer across every four attention layers instead of computing one per layer.
bullets: Cuts per-token FLOPs by 2.9x at a 1M-token context length compared to indexing every layer independently
MoE routing activates only 40B of the 744B total parameters per token, keeping serving cost down despite the model's size
Ships in BF16 and FP8 precision for different deployment budgets

slides.title: Beats GPT-5.5 on Coding, at a Fraction of the Price
slides.body: GLM-5.2's list pricing and SWE-Bench Pro score, compared against GPT-5.5's.
bullets: SWE-Bench Pro: GLM-5.2 scores 62.1 vs. GPT-5.5's 58.6
Input pricing: roughly $1.40/M tokens vs. GPT-5.5's $5/M
Output pricing: roughly $4.40/M tokens vs. GPT-5.5's $30/M — about a sixth of the combined cost

slides.title: What a 1M-Token Window Actually Buys an Agent
slides.body: A mid-sized codebase can easily run 200K+ tokens of source. Add a long agentic session's tool-call history on top, and shorter-context models are forced to summarize or re-fetch files repeatedly.
bullets: With 1M tokens, an agent can hold an entire mid-sized repo plus 500+ turns of tool history without truncation
A 128K-256K model working the same task has to drop old context, risking it forgetting earlier decisions or file contents
IndexShare is what makes serving that much context economically viable instead of just theoretically possible

slides.title: Open Weights Don't Mean Free — or Simple
slides.body: Beating a closed model on a benchmark and being cheap to run in practice aren't the same thing.
bullets: Self-hosting a 744B-parameter model (even with 40B active) needs serious multi-GPU infrastructure most teams don't have
Third-party hosted pricing varies a lot in practice — the same model has been listed anywhere from about $0.95 to $3.00 per million input tokens depending on provider
Sparse attention's savings are biggest at very long context; on short prompts the efficiency edge over dense models shrinks

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: GLM-5.2 is a concrete data point that open-weight models have closed much of the cost and capability gap with closed frontier models on agentic coding.
bullets: IndexShare-based sparse attention is the specific trick making a stable 1M-token context affordable to serve
It outscored GPT-5.5 on SWE-Bench Pro while costing roughly a sixth as much per token at list price
Apache-2.0 licensing means it's usable commercially — but running it well still requires either serious infra or a hosted provider

options: It cannot call external tools
Self-hosting the full model needs serious multi-GPU infrastructure, and third-party hosted pricing varies widely by provider
It has no usable license for commercial work
It cannot handle code at all
questions.explanation: 744B total parameters (even with only 40B active) is not something most teams can self-host cheaply, and observed third-party pricing for the same model has ranged roughly 2-3x depending on the provider.

posts.title: Attention Sinks: Why the First Tokens Never Leave the Cache
posts.subtitle: StreamingLLM keeps a handful of tokens pinned so infinite generation doesn't blow up
posts.summary: StreamingLLM found that the first few tokens of any sequence absorb a disproportionate share of attention regardless of their content, acting as a 'sink' for softmax probability mass. Pinning those tokens in the KV cache while sliding a window over the rest keeps memory bounded and perplexity flat, letting models like Llama-2 and Falcon stream past 4 million tokens without retraining.

slides.title: Attention Sinks: The Tokens Every Long Chat Secretly Depends On
slides.body: Discovered while trying to make LLMs generate indefinitely without their memory usage growing forever — the fix turned out to be almost absurdly small.
bullets: The trick: never evict the first ~4 tokens from the KV cache
Lets Llama-2, MPT, Falcon, and Pythia stream stably past 4 million tokens
No retraining or architecture change required — it's a caching policy

slides.title: Naive Sliding-Window Attention Falls Apart
slides.body: A full KV cache grows with every generated token — unbounded memory for a conversation or agent loop that never ends. The obvious fix, a fixed-size sliding window, breaks in a surprising way.
bullets: Full cache: memory grows O(n) with sequence length — infeasible for truly long-running generation
Sliding window: keep only the most recent L tokens' key/value pairs, drop the rest
Result: perplexity explodes the moment the very first token slides out of the window — even though that token wasn't semantically important

slides.title: The Fix: Pin a Few 'Sink' Tokens, Slide the Rest
slides.body: Softmax attention scores must sum to 1 even when no key is a good semantic match for the query — so models learn to dump that leftover probability mass onto early tokens, regardless of what those tokens actually say.
bullets: Researchers found the first ~4 tokens absorb a disproportionate share of attention across most heads and layers, purely as a side effect of softmax normalization
StreamingLLM's SinkAttention keeps those first tokens in the cache permanently
Everything else uses a normal sliding window of recent tokens — cache size stays fixed regardless of how long generation runs

slides.title: A Chat That Runs for Millions of Tokens
slides.body: Picture an agent loop or chatbot session that just keeps going — no restart, no summarization step.
bullets: Cache holds a small fixed set of sink tokens plus the most recent window of tokens (window size is a serving-time configuration choice)
Total cache size never grows past that fixed budget, no matter how long the session runs
Perplexity stays flat through the transition, instead of spiking the moment the original prompt tokens get pushed out

slides.title: Three Approaches to Long-Running Generation
slides.body: How each caching strategy handles memory and stability once a sequence outgrows the initial context.
bullets: Dense (full cache): numerically stable, but memory grows without bound
Sliding window alone: bounded memory, but breaks the instant the first token is evicted
StreamingLLM (sink + window): bounded memory and stays stable indefinitely

rows: Stable, but eventually runs out of memory
Perplexity explodes once first token is evicted
Stays stable past millions of tokens

slides.title: Where Attention Sinks Don't Help
slides.body: This is a stability fix, not a memory upgrade — it's easy to mistake the two.
bullets: It doesn't recover evicted information — the model genuinely can't recall specific facts pushed out of the sliding window
It's not a substitute for real long-context architectures when you actually need to reference far-back content precisely
Best suited to open-ended serving scenarios (chatbots, agent loops) where staying stable matters more than perfectly remembering the start of a very old conversation

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: A handful of tokens act as attention sinks purely because softmax attention needs somewhere to put unused probability mass — and that turns out to be exploitable.
bullets: Never evicting the first few tokens, while sliding a window over the rest, keeps KV cache memory bounded indefinitely
It's a cheap, retraining-free fix for a subtle failure mode in streaming generation
It buys stability, not memory — evicted content is genuinely gone, not just deprioritized

questions.prompt: Why does perplexity explode when using a naive sliding window with no sink tokens?
options: The model runs out of GPU memory
Evicting the very first tokens removes something the attention mechanism structurally relies on, even though those tokens aren't semantically special
The tokenizer produces invalid tokens once the window slides
The model's context window size was set too small
questions.explanation: Softmax attention needs somewhere to put probability mass when no key is a strong match. Models learn to dump that leftover mass onto the first few tokens as a side effect — so removing them breaks the attention computation, regardless of what those tokens actually contain.

questions.prompt: What does StreamingLLM do differently from plain sliding-window attention?
options: It simply increases the window size
It permanently keeps a few initial 'sink' tokens in the KV cache alongside a sliding window of recent tokens
It retrains the model from scratch with a new objective
It removes attention computation for older tokens entirely
questions.explanation: SinkAttention pins the first ~4 tokens in the cache permanently and applies a normal sliding window to everything after them — a small caching policy change, not an architecture or training change.

questions.prompt: What's a real limitation of the attention-sink approach?
options: It can't run on GPU hardware
It doesn't let the model actually recall specific facts that were evicted from the sliding window — it only keeps generation numerically stable
It only works on models named Llama
It requires more memory than keeping a full, unbounded KV cache
questions.explanation: Attention sinks fix a stability problem, not a memory problem. Content that falls out of the sliding window is genuinely gone from the model's cache — the technique just prevents the model from breaking down numerically when that happens.

posts.title: Frontis-MA1: A 35B Model That Improves Its Own Training Pipeline
posts.subtitle: Recursive self-improvement, made executable on a single RTX 4090
posts.summary: Frontis-MA1 is a 35B open-weight model trained to improve the process of building AI itself: it drafts, debugs, and evolves machine-learning programs, lifting MLE-Bench Lite Medal Average from 39.39% to 71.21% on one consumer GPU. The team open-sourced the entire OpenMLE stack — gym, RL, and evolutionary search — making 'AI improving AI' something you can reproduce, not just read about.

slides.title: Can an AI Get Better at Building AI?
slides.body: Frontis-MA1 turns 'recursive self-improvement' from a thought experiment into a benchmarked, reproducible system — running on a single 12GB gaming GPU.

slides.title: RSI Talk Has Outrun RSI Evidence
slides.body: "Recursive self-improvement" gets invoked constantly, but almost nobody could point to a task where you feed an AI system's own output back into training it and measure a clean, repeatable win.
bullets: Machine learning engineering (MLE) is a natural testbed: writing/debugging/tuning ML code is verifiable — you can just run it and score the result
Prior agent-coding work mostly stops at 'write code once'; it doesn't close the loop back into the model's own training
No shared, open benchmark existed for measuring whether a model's self-improvement loop actually compounds

slides.title: OpenMLE: Four Operators, One Closed Loop
slides.body: The team built OpenMLE, a full open stack spanning task environments, RL training, and evolutionary search, then post-trained Frontis-MA1 (35B) as a meta-evolution agent inside it.
bullets: Four atomic operators the model learns: Draft (write from scratch), Improve (refine using execution feedback), Debug (repair failing code), Crossover (recombine two working solutions)
Operators are trained with execution-grounded supervised fine-tuning plus online RL, on data deduplicated against every eval benchmark
The trained operators are then composed into long-horizon evolutionary search — 'search produces experience, experience enters training, trained models return to search'

slides.title: 39.39% → 71.21% Medal Average
slides.body: All numbers are on MLE-Bench Lite under a fixed 12-hour-per-task budget, capped at a single RTX 4090 (12GB VRAM) — not a data-center cluster.
bullets: Base 35B model alone: 39.39% Medal Average
+ OpenMLE-Evo search: 60.61%
+ OpenMLE-Evo-Max (full budget): 71.21% — approaching GPT-5.6 Sol and the 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3, and beating GPT-5.5 + Codex
Held-out NatureBench transfer: swapping in a new base model still lifted Match-SOTA 50%→70%; swapping the whole framework lifted it 20%→50%

slides.title: Watching One Evolution Round
slides.body: Picture a single MLE-Bench task: 'build a better tabular classifier.'
bullets: Draft: the agent writes three candidate pipelines from scratch, each scored by actually running them
Improve: the best-scoring draft gets refined using its own execution logs (e.g. 'validation loss spiked at epoch 4 — add early stopping')
Crossover: a second lineage's feature-engineering step is spliced into the first lineage's model architecture
Debug: a broken crossover (shape mismatch) gets auto-repaired using the stack trace as feedback — no human in the loop

slides.title: Why 'AI4AI' Is a Different Claim Than 'Coding Agent'
slides.body: A coding agent writes code you asked for once. An AI4AI system is scored on whether repeated self-directed cycles actually compound — the entire point is the delta between round 1 and round N.
bullets: The Medal Average curve (39%→60%→71%) is itself the evidence, not a single benchmark score
Held-out transfer to NatureBench matters more than the headline number — it shows the learned operators generalize, not just memorize MLE-Bench's specific tasks
Running the whole loop on a 12GB consumer GPU is a deliberate constraint: it argues self-improvement doesn't require frontier-lab compute to study

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Frontis-MA1 doesn't claim general recursive self-improvement — it claims a measurable, reproducible slice of it inside ML engineering, with the code to check the work yourself.
bullets: 35B model + evolutionary search beat a 12-hour compute budget's naive baseline by 32 points of Medal Average
The gains transfer to a held-out benchmark, evidence the operators learned something general rather than overfitting
Full OpenMLE stack (gym, RL, evolutionary search, 1.2M+ task instances) is open-sourced under CC BY-NC 4.0
This is a research testbed, not a production system — 12-hour budgets and MLE-Bench-style tasks are narrower than real-world ML engineering

questions.prompt: What does Frontis-MA1's Medal Average go from and to on MLE-Bench Lite as compute (search) is added?
questions.explanation: The base 35B model alone scores 39.39%; adding OpenMLE-Evo search raises it to 60.61%, and the full OpenMLE-Evo-Max budget reaches 71.21% — the curve itself is the paper's central evidence for compounding self-improvement.

questions.prompt: What are the four atomic operators Frontis-MA1 is trained around?
options: Plan, Act, Reflect, Retry
Draft, Improve, Debug, Crossover
Search, Rank, Filter, Select
Encode, Decode, Attend, Predict
questions.explanation: Draft writes a program from scratch, Improve refines it with execution feedback, Debug repairs failures using stack traces, and Crossover recombines two working solutions — all four are trained via execution-grounded SFT plus RL, then composed into evolutionary search.

questions.prompt: Why does the NatureBench transfer result matter more than the headline MLE-Bench number?
options: It's a bigger benchmark so it's more prestigious
It shows the learned operators generalize rather than just memorizing MLE-Bench's specific tasks
It was scored by a human panel instead of automated execution
It used a larger GPU budget
questions.explanation: Swapping in a new base model or a new framework and still seeing Match-SOTA improve (50%→70% and 20%→50% respectively) on a held-out benchmark is the strongest evidence that the operators learned a transferable skill, not a benchmark-specific trick.

posts.title: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731: Beating the Bigger Model With Zero New Architecture
posts.subtitle: Same weights shape, same size — the entire agentic jump came from post-training
posts.summary: DeepSeek shipped the official V4-Flash-0731 build on July 31, 2026 — identical architecture to the earlier preview, purely re-post-trained — and it now beats the larger V4-Pro-Preview on Terminal Bench 2.1, DeepSWE, and Cybergym. It's a clean public data point for how much capability is currently sitting in post-training, not parameter count.

slides.title: The Small Model Just Beat the Big One
slides.body: No new architecture. No new parameters. DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 out-scores its own bigger sibling on agentic coding benchmarks — purely from post-training.

slides.title: The Assumption This Breaks
slides.body: The default mental model for AI progress is 'bigger/newer architecture = better.' DeepSeek's own product lineup just contradicted that inside a single family.
bullets: V4-Flash-0731 keeps the exact same architecture and parameter count as the earlier V4-Flash-Preview
The only change: it was re-post-trained — new supervised fine-tuning and RL passes, no pretraining or architecture changes
Despite being the cheaper, smaller-tier model, it now surpasses V4-Pro-Preview — the larger model in the same family — on several agentic coding benchmarks

slides.title: The Numbers, Same Weights Shape
slides.body: Scores on agentic/coding benchmarks reported in DeepSeek's official API changelog for the July 31, 2026 build.
bullets: Terminal Bench 2.1: 82.7
DeepSWE: 54.4
Cybergym: 76.7
Pricing unchanged: $0.14 / 1M input tokens (uncached), $0.28 / 1M output tokens — a third of V4-Pro's rate

slides.title: What 'Only Post-Training' Actually Means Here
slides.body: Post-training is everything that happens after the base model finishes pretraining: supervised fine-tuning on curated trajectories, then reinforcement learning against verifiable rewards (tests passing, terminal tasks completing).
bullets: For agentic coding specifically, RL rewards can be objective: did the test suite pass, did the terminal command actually accomplish the task
That objectivity lets you run many more RL iterations productively than on fuzzier tasks like open-ended chat
The build also natively supports OpenAI's Responses API format and is specifically adapted for Codex-style tool-calling harnesses

slides.title: Why This Matters If You're Choosing a Model
slides.body: Imagine you picked V4-Pro-Preview last month because it was DeepSeek's flagship agentic option.
bullets: As of July 31, the cheaper V4-Flash-0731 beats it on the exact coding/terminal benchmarks you cared about
Your API call doesn't even need to change — same model name (deepseek-v4-flash) now resolves to the improved build
The lesson generalizes: 'which tier is smartest' in a model family can flip between snapshots without a version-number change signaling it

slides.title: Tradeoffs and What to Watch
slides.body: Post-training gains are real but they compound on top of whatever the base architecture supports — they're not unlimited.
bullets: This is a snapshot comparison (Flash-0731 vs. Pro-Preview, not the final Pro GA) — DeepSeek's V4-Pro GA build may reclaim the lead
Benchmark wins on Terminal Bench / DeepSWE / Cybergym are agentic-coding-specific; they don't guarantee broader reasoning or knowledge gains
'Same architecture, better post-training' is a cheaper lever than pretraining a bigger model — expect labs to lean on it more as pretraining compute costs keep rising

questions.prompt: What actually changed between V4-Flash-Preview and the official V4-Flash-0731 build?
options: The parameter count was doubled
A new attention architecture was introduced
Only post-training (SFT + RL) — architecture and size stayed identical
The context window was extended to 10M tokens
questions.explanation: DeepSeek stated the 0731 build kept the exact same architecture and size as the preview and was only re-post-trained — the agentic capability jump came entirely from SFT and RL, not from scaling up.

questions.prompt: Why can RL push agentic coding performance further than it typically pushes open-ended chat quality?
options: Coding tasks have objective, verifiable rewards (tests pass or fail) that support many clean RL iterations
Coding models are always larger than chat models
RL doesn't actually help coding, only pretraining does
Chat tasks have more available training data
questions.explanation: Agentic coding rewards can be objective — did the test suite pass, did the terminal task complete — which makes RL signal cleaner and more scalable than for fuzzier open-ended generation tasks.

questions.prompt: What should you NOT conclude from V4-Flash-0731 beating V4-Pro-Preview on these benchmarks?
options: That post-training can meaningfully close capability gaps within a model family
That Flash is now unconditionally the better model for every task, forever
That the same architecture can yield different capability depending on post-training
That RL on verifiable coding rewards is a productive lever
questions.explanation: This is a snapshot result on specific agentic coding benchmarks against a Preview build, not GA — it doesn't establish permanent, universal superiority over every future or non-coding comparison.

posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Why Modern LLMs Stopped Using All Their Parameters
posts.subtitle: How routing tokens to a handful of specialists gives you a bigger brain for the same compute bill
posts.summary: Mixture of Experts (MoE) replaces a single dense feed-forward block with many smaller 'expert' networks and a router that activates only a few per token. It's why DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, and Kimi K3 can have hundreds of billions of total parameters while only paying compute for a fraction of them at inference time — with a real cost in memory footprint and routing complexity.

slides.title: A Model With 671B Parameters That Only Uses 37B at a Time
slides.body: That's not a bug — it's Mixture of Experts, the architecture behind most of today's frontier open models.

slides.title: Dense Models Force a Bad Tradeoff
slides.body: In a standard 'dense' transformer, every parameter runs on every token. Want more knowledge/capacity? You pay for it on every single forward pass, whether that token needed it or not.
bullets: Scaling a dense model means compute cost and parameter count rise together — there's no way to add capacity without also adding latency and FLOPs
But most tokens don't need most of the model's knowledge at once — a token about French grammar doesn't need the same weights as one about Python syntax
Dense scaling was hitting a wall: bigger dense models became too slow and expensive to serve at scale

slides.title: Route Instead of Run Everything
slides.body: MoE replaces each dense feed-forward layer with many smaller expert networks plus a lightweight router. For each token, the router picks a small subset of experts to actually run.
bullets: A router (usually a small linear layer + softmax) scores every expert per token and picks the top-k, e.g. top-2 of 8, or top-8 of 256
Only the selected experts' weights are used for that token — the rest sit idle for this forward pass
Attention layers and sometimes a 'shared expert' stay dense (every token uses them); it's specifically the feed-forward blocks that go sparse
Total parameters = capacity/knowledge; active parameters = what you actually pay in compute per token

slides.title: Total vs. Active Parameters, Real Models
slides.body: The gap between the two columns is the whole point of MoE — capacity without a proportional compute bill.
bullets: Mixtral 8x7B: 8 experts per layer, top-2 routing — ~47B total, ~13B active per token, matching Llama-2 70B quality at roughly 13B-model compute cost
DeepSeek-V3: 256 routed experts + 1 shared expert, top-8 routing — 671B total, only 37B active per token
Both models cost roughly what their 'active' number suggests to run, while storing roughly what their 'total' number suggests

slides.title: Following One Token Through the Router
slides.body: Say the token "def" appears at the start of a Python function inside a long prompt that's mostly English prose.
bullets: The router looks at that token's hidden state and scores all 256 experts in the layer
It picks the top-8 highest-scoring experts — likely ones that, over training, specialized toward code-like patterns — plus the always-on shared expert
Only those 9 experts' feed-forward weights actually multiply against this token; the other 248 experts do zero work for it
The next token, mid-sentence in the English prose, might route to a completely different set of 8 experts

slides.title: Load Balancing: The Hard Part Nobody Sees
slides.body: If left alone, routers tend to collapse onto a favorite handful of experts, starving the rest — bad for both training signal and inference throughput.
bullets: Early MoE systems (e.g. Switch Transformer, GShard) added an auxiliary load-balancing loss that penalizes uneven expert usage
DeepSeek-V3 popularized an auxiliary-loss-free balancing strategy: a learned per-expert bias term nudges routing decisions without polluting the main training loss
Poor load balancing shows up as some experts being memory-hot and others nearly untrained — directly hurting quality, not just efficiency

slides.title: Tradeoffs and When It's Not Worth It
slides.body: MoE isn't a strict upgrade — it trades one bottleneck (compute) for others (memory and engineering complexity).
bullets: You still need to hold ALL experts in memory even though only a few run per token — MoE saves compute, not VRAM/RAM footprint
Routing adds real engineering complexity: load balancing, expert-parallel serving infrastructure, and harder fine-tuning dynamics than a dense model
For small models or latency-insensitive single-GPU deployments where memory is the binding constraint, a dense model of the 'active' size is often simpler and just as practical
MoE wins when you're serving at scale and can amortize the memory cost across many concurrent requests, or when you need capacity a dense model can't afford to run

questions.prompt: In a Mixture of Experts layer, what determines which experts process a given token?
options: Every expert always processes every token
A router scores the experts for that token and selects a top-k subset to run
Experts are chosen randomly each forward pass
The user manually selects which expert to use
questions.explanation: A lightweight router (typically a linear layer + softmax) scores all experts for each token's hidden state and activates only the top-k highest-scoring ones — that sparsity is what makes MoE cheaper than a dense model of equivalent total size.

questions.prompt: DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total parameters but only 37B active per token. What does 'active' govern?
options: How much disk space the model needs
How much compute/FLOPs are spent processing that specific token
How many tokens fit in the context window
How many GPUs are required to download the model
questions.explanation: Active parameters are the ones actually multiplied against a given token's hidden state — they determine the compute cost per token. Total parameters still all need to be stored in memory, since any token could route to any expert.

questions.prompt: Why do MoE models need a load-balancing mechanism during training?
options: To make the model output shorter responses
To prevent the router from collapsing onto a small set of favorite experts, leaving others undertrained
To reduce the total parameter count
To speed up tokenization
questions.explanation: Without balancing, routers tend to concentrate traffic on a few experts early in training, which both starves other experts of gradient signal and creates uneven load at serving time. DeepSeek-V3's auxiliary-loss-free approach uses a learned per-expert bias instead of an extra loss term to fix this.

posts.title: Gemini 3.6 Flash: Doing More Agentic Work Per Token
posts.subtitle: Google's new 'workhorse' model cuts output tokens 17% and passes the savings straight to price
posts.summary: On July 21, 2026, Google DeepMind shipped Gemini 3.6 Flash alongside 3.5 Flash-Lite and a cybersecurity-focused 3.5 Flash Cyber. The headline change isn't raw intelligence — it's efficiency: 17% fewer output tokens than 3.5 Flash, a price cut that follows, the same 1M-token context window, and wins on Google's own coding/agentic benchmarks.

bullets: Ships as a trio: 3.6 Flash (general workhorse), 3.5 Flash-Lite (cheapest), 3.5 Flash Cyber (security-tuned)
Available immediately via the Gemini app, Google Search, Google AI Studio, and the Gemini API
Positioned explicitly for agentic workflows and app/web development, not chat-first use
slides.body: Gemini 3.6 Flash is Google DeepMind's mid-tier model refresh, launched July 21, 2026 alongside Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and a cybersecurity-specialized Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber. It's built for the workloads that run constantly, not the ones that need maximum reasoning.
slides.title: A 'workhorse' release, not a flagship one

bullets: Multi-step tool-calling agents pay for every intermediate 'thought' and tool response, not just the final answer
A model that's 10% cheaper per token but needs 30% more tokens to finish a task is a net loss
3.5 Flash was already Google's efficiency tier — 3.6 Flash had to beat it on tokens-per-task, not just price
slides.body: A coding agent that reads a repo, calls tools, and iterates can burn hundreds of thousands of tokens per task before it ever asks a hard reasoning question. At that volume, output-token price and token-efficiency matter more than another point of benchmark accuracy.
slides.title: Agentic loops burn tokens whether or not the model gets smarter

bullets: Output price: $9.00 → $7.50 per million tokens (~17% cheaper)
Input price unchanged at $1.50 per million tokens
Context window unchanged at 1,048,576 tokens, max output 65,536 tokens
Knowledge cutoff moved forward to March 2026
slides.body: Google says 3.6 Flash needs 17% fewer output tokens than 3.5 Flash to do comparable work. Output pricing dropped from $9.00 to $7.50 per million tokens; input price held steady at $1.50 per million tokens.
slides.title: 17% fewer output tokens, and the savings get passed through

slides.body: Google published four head-to-head coding and agentic benchmarks. The margins aren't uniform — some are close, one is enormous.

rows: Output tokens needed for comparable work

slides.title: 3.5 Flash vs. 3.6 Flash, head to head

bullets: At 3.5 Flash pricing, a task generating 500K output tokens across that loop cost $4.50
The same task on 3.6 Flash, needing ~17% fewer tokens to reach the same result, costs roughly $3.10 — output-price cut and token-efficiency gain compound
The +37 point DeepSWE gain matters here specifically: DeepSWE-style tasks are long, multi-file coding loops — exactly the shape of this workload
slides.body: Take an agent doing an automated code-review pass over a large PR: it loads diff context, calls a linter tool, reads test output, and drafts comments — a loop that might run 40-60 tool calls before finishing.
slides.title: What this means for a repo-scale coding agent

bullets: Good fit: agentic coding loops, high-volume tool-calling, latency-sensitive app features
Not the fit: tasks that need frontier-level reasoning depth — that's still a Pro-tier model's job
A 17% token-efficiency claim is workload-dependent; short single-turn prompts will see less benefit than long agentic loops
The parallel launch of a cybersecurity-specific variant (3.5 Flash Cyber) signals Google is now splitting Flash by use case, not just by size
slides.body: 3.6 Flash is a lateral efficiency upgrade, not a reasoning upgrade. Google shipped it as the model you route high-volume, well-scoped work to — not the one you send your hardest problem to.
slides.title: It's still a Flash-tier model — know when to reach for it

questions.prompt: What is the primary improvement Google is claiming for Gemini 3.6 Flash over 3.5 Flash?
options: A larger context window
17% fewer output tokens needed for comparable work, with output pricing cut to match
A completely new model architecture
Free unlimited usage for developers
questions.explanation: 3.6 Flash keeps the same 1M-token context window and input price. The headline change is token efficiency (17% fewer output tokens) paired with a matching output-price cut from $9.00 to $7.50 per million tokens.

questions.prompt: On which benchmark did Gemini 3.6 Flash show its largest published margin over 3.5 Flash?
options: SWE-Bench Pro, by 4.5 points
DeepSWE, by 37 points
A general knowledge benchmark
Google didn't publish any comparative benchmarks
questions.explanation: Google published four head-to-head benchmarks; the SWE-Bench Pro gain was a modest 4.5 points, while the DeepSWE gain was a much larger 37 points — DeepSWE-style long, multi-file coding tasks are where the efficiency gains compound most visibly.

questions.prompt: Why might token-efficiency gains matter more for agentic workloads than for single-turn chat?
options: Agentic loops make many tool calls and generate many intermediate outputs, so per-token savings compound across the whole task
Chat responses are always longer than agent outputs
Token efficiency only affects input tokens, which chat doesn't use
There's no meaningful difference between the two workload types
questions.explanation: A single chat reply generates one block of output tokens. An agentic loop generates many rounds of tool calls, tool results, and intermediate reasoning — so a per-token efficiency gain multiplies across dozens of turns instead of applying once.

posts.title: PhiZero: Teaching a World Model to Reason Before It Renders
posts.subtitle: Instead of predicting pixels directly, this model first 'thinks' in a learned language of physical state changes
posts.summary: Researchers from CASIA's NLPR lab propose PhiZero, a world model built around 'physical language' — a compact, discrete, self-supervised representation of how physical states transition over time. Instead of predicting future video frames directly in pixel space, PhiZero first reasons in this symbolic language, then renders the result, and reports the best scores on three physics-focused world-model benchmarks: Physics-IQ Verified, PhyGround, and WorldModelBench.

bullets: Introduces 'physical language': a compact discrete representation of world-state transitions
Learned entirely through self-supervision on in-the-wild, unlabeled video
Authors: Shuyao Shang, Yuqi Wang, Ruopeng Gao, Xu Chen, Tieniu Tan, Lue Fan, Zhaoxiang Zhang (arXiv 2607.28624)
slides.body: PhiZero, from NLPR/CASIA (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences), separates 'what happens next, physically' from 'what that looks like rendered' — two problems that pixel-space video models normally solve as one.
slides.title: Most video world models predict pixels; this one predicts physics first

bullets: Errors in physical plausibility only show up after the (expensive) pixels are already generated
Implicit dynamics don't transfer cleanly — you can't 'reuse' a physical pattern the way you can reuse a symbolic token
Long-horizon rollouts drift, because nothing forces the model to commit to a consistent state-transition plan first
slides.body: Standard video world models generate the next frames directly in pixel space. Physical dynamics — momentum, collision, gravity, occlusion — are implicit in the weights, never made explicit, so there's no intermediate representation to inspect, reuse, or reason over before rendering happens.
slides.title: Predicting pixels directly hides the reasoning it depends on

bullets: Self-supervised: learned from raw, in-the-wild video, not simulation or annotated data
Discrete and compact — a sequence of physical-language tokens, not a dense latent vector
Captures state-transition patterns that recur across very different visual scenes
slides.body: PhiZero learns a discrete token vocabulary — physical language — that captures recurring state-transition patterns (a ball leaving a surface, an object occluding another) purely from watching unlabeled video, no physics engine or labels involved.
slides.title: Physical language: a vocabulary for how the world changes

bullets: Stage 1 (reason): predict the future as physical-language tokens, conditioned on the observed video
Stage 2 (render): decode the predicted physical-language sequence into pixel-space video
Because reasoning happens in a small discrete space first, the model commits to a physically coherent plan before spending compute on pixels
slides.body: PhiZero first infers how the world will evolve as a physical-language sequence — an explicit reasoning step — and only then renders that sequence into actual video frames. Dynamics inference and pixel synthesis become separate, inspectable stages.

bullets: Example: a bouncing-and-rolling motion pattern learned from one video can be applied to a different object or background at inference time
This works because the 'reasoning' stage output — the physical-language sequence — is decoupled from any single scene's pixels
The paper reports this as one of PhiZero's demonstrated capabilities, alongside fine-grained action-conditioned simulation
slides.body: Because dynamics are captured as reusable physical-language tokens rather than baked into pixel predictions for one specific scene, a motion pattern learned in one context can be replayed onto a scene the model never saw that motion applied to.
slides.title: Zero-shot motion transfer

bullets: No formal physical guarantees: the tokens capture statistical regularities in video, not verified physics equations
Two-stage reason-then-render pipeline adds architectural and inference overhead versus a single end-to-end pixel model
Quality is bounded by the diversity of the in-the-wild video it self-supervised on — rare or exotic physical interactions may not have a clean token vocabulary
Best fit today: research and simulation contexts that value physical coherence over raw generation speed
slides.body: PhiZero's 'physical language' is discovered from data, not hand-designed — powerful for generality, but it inherits the same limits as any learned representation.
slides.title: A learned physics vocabulary, not a physics engine

questions.prompt: What is 'physical language' in PhiZero?
options: A natural-language description written by human annotators
A compact, discrete representation of world-state transitions, learned self-supervised from video
A physics simulation engine bundled with the model
The model's system prompt describing physics rules
questions.explanation: Physical language is a learned, discrete token vocabulary that captures recurring patterns of how the physical world changes state — learned entirely through self-supervision on unlabeled video, with no physics engine or human labels involved.

questions.prompt: How does the 'reason-then-render' paradigm differ from standard pixel-space video world models?
options: It skips rendering entirely and only outputs text
It predicts pixels first, then explains the physics afterward
It first predicts future world evolution as physical-language tokens, then renders that sequence into video — separating dynamics inference from pixel synthesis
It requires a human to manually specify the physics before generation
questions.explanation: Standard models predict pixels directly with dynamics left implicit. PhiZero makes dynamics an explicit, separate reasoning target — predicting a physical-language sequence first — before a second stage renders that plan into pixels.

questions.prompt: What is a real limitation of PhiZero's approach, according to the paper's design?
options: It cannot generate any video at all
Its physical-language vocabulary is learned from data, so it offers no formal physics guarantees and is bounded by the diversity of its training video
It only works on synthetic, simulated scenes
It requires labeled physics annotations for every training video
questions.explanation: Because physical language is discovered via self-supervision rather than derived from physics equations, PhiZero has no formal correctness guarantees — its ability to model rare or unusual physical interactions depends on how well those interactions were represented in the in-the-wild video it learned from.

posts.title: Context Rot: Why a Bigger Context Window Isn't a Bigger Budget
posts.subtitle: Every frontier model tested gets measurably worse as you fill up its context — long before you hit the token limit
posts.summary: Context rot is the measurable drop in an LLM's output quality as input length grows — even well inside the model's stated context limit. Chroma's research testing 18 frontier models found every one degrades non-uniformly, with accuracy drops of 30-50% well before the documented ceiling, driven by lost-in-the-middle attention patterns and quadratic attention dilution. The fix isn't a bigger window; it's treating context as a curated budget.

bullets: Tested at every input-length increment, not just at the documented maximum
Degradation happens well before the model hits its stated context limit
This isn't one model's flaw — it showed up across every frontier model tested
slides.body: It's tempting to treat a large context window like free storage: just put everything in and let the model sort it out. Chroma Research tested that assumption across 18 frontier models — including GPT-4.1, Claude Opus 4, and Gemini 2.5 — and found every single one degrades as input length grows.
slides.title: A 1M-token window doesn't mean 1M tokens of equal attention

bullets: For coding agents specifically, context rot is described as the primary failure mode, not an edge case
The drop is non-uniform: it's not a smooth, predictable decline, so it's easy to miss in casual testing
A model can pass a short-context version of a task and fail the identical task once padded with unrelated context
slides.body: Developers routinely stuff entire codebases, chat histories, or document sets into context, assuming a bigger window only helps. But accuracy on the same task can drop 30-50% purely from adding more (even relevant) surrounding text — not from the answer becoming harder to find.
slides.title: The intuition 'more context = strictly better' is wrong

bullets: Lost-in-the-middle: models attend well to the start and end of context but poorly to the middle, producing accuracy drops of 30%+ when the relevant information sits mid-context
Attention dilution: self-attention is quadratic in sequence length — 100K tokens means roughly 10 billion pairwise token relationships competing for the same fixed 'attention budget'
Together they mean position, not just presence, determines whether the model actually uses a piece of context
slides.body: Context rot isn't mysterious — it traces to two structural properties of how transformers process long sequences.
slides.title: Two mechanisms, one outcome

bullets: The constraint didn't change; only its position in context did
This is why agent frameworks increasingly re-inject critical instructions near the end of long-running sessions
The same effect explains why RAG systems that dump 20 retrieved chunks in the middle of a prompt can underperform ones that surface the top 3 clearly
slides.body: Imagine a 200-turn coding-agent session where message #3 states a hard constraint: 'always run the test suite before committing.' By turn 150, that instruction is now deep in the middle of a long context — and lost-in-the-middle attention means the agent is measurably more likely to skip it than if the same instruction had been restated near the end.
slides.title: A buried instruction gets silently dropped

slides.body: The practical fork in the road: treat the context window as unlimited storage, or treat it as a scarce, positioned resource.

rows: Simple to implement, no retrieval step needed
Accuracy drops 30-50% as irrelevant/mid-buried content accumulates
Only relevant chunks enter context, positioned deliberately
Adds retrieval-quality as a new dependency; recall matters
Keeps long-running agent sessions short and current
Risks summarizing away a detail that turns out to matter later

slides.title: Stuffing context vs. curating it

bullets: Prefer retrieval over stuffing: put only what's relevant into context, not everything that might be
Place critical instructions and facts near the start or end of context, not buried in the middle
For long-running agents, periodically compact or summarize context rather than letting it grow unbounded
Don't assume a documented context limit is a performance guarantee — test task accuracy at the input lengths you'll actually use
slides.body: The fix for context rot isn't a bigger model or a bigger window — both still exhibit the same pattern. It's discipline about what goes in and where.
slides.title: Treat the context window as a budget, not a bucket

questions.prompt: What did Chroma's research find when testing 18 frontier LLMs across increasing input lengths?
options: Performance stayed flat until the exact documented context limit was reached
Every model tested showed measurable performance degradation as input length grew, well before hitting the stated limit
Only smaller, less capable models showed degradation
Longer context always improved accuracy
questions.explanation: The research found this pattern across every model tested, including top frontier models like GPT-4.1, Claude Opus 4, and Gemini 2.5 — degradation is a structural property of how these models process long context, not a gap specific to weaker models.

questions.prompt: What is the 'lost-in-the-middle' effect?
options: Models forget the entire conversation after a certain length
Models attend well to the start and end of context but poorly to information positioned in the middle
A bug that only affects open-source models
The model literally deletes middle tokens from memory
questions.explanation: Lost-in-the-middle describes an attention pattern where models reliably favor content near the start and end of their context window, causing accuracy drops of 30%+ when the answer or relevant instruction sits in the middle.

questions.prompt: Which practice best mitigates context rot in a long-running agent session?
options: Maximizing the context window size and stuffing in every possible piece of information
Retrieving and curating only relevant content, and periodically compacting or re-positioning critical instructions
Ignoring the problem since bigger models will eventually solve it
Always placing the most important information in the exact middle of the prompt
questions.explanation: Because attention degrades with length and position, the practical mitigation is curation: retrieve only what's relevant, compact long sessions periodically, and keep critical instructions near the start or end rather than the middle.
